guest_memfd-backed guest that faults past the first 4K of a page can
find its neighbour's mapping, get -EAGAIN and take the same fault
forever.

The memory fault exit reports s2fd->fault_ipa too, which for a nested
guest's fault is the nested IPA rather than the canonical one
kvm_gmem_get_pfn() failed on.

Take the addresses from kvm_s2_fault_vma_info instead, as
user_mem_abort() does, and report the canonical gfn in the memory fault
exit. kvm_s2_fault_get_vma_info() itself isn't called: a guest_memfd
memslot's userspace_addr doesn't need to be backed by a VMA.

items.title: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: nvme-tcp: Validate the queue state under the queue…
items.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nvme-tcp: Validate the queue state under the queue lock in the address attribute

Reading the "address" sysfs attribute calls kernel_getsockname() on the
admin queue socket, which can race with the queue teardown during
connection error recovery: a reader can observe NVME_TCP_Q_LIVE set,
then block on the queue lock while nvme_tcp_free_queue() releases the
socket and clears queue->sock without holding the lock.  Once the
reader acquires the lock it dereferences the NULL socket pointer.

Commit 76d54bf20cdc ("nvme-tcp: don't access released socket during
error recovery") had the queue liveness check inside the lock.
Commit 782373ba2766 ("nvme: tcp: avoid race between queue_lock lock
and destroy") moved it back out because the lock itself is destroyed
in nvme_tcp_free_queue(), so a reader arriving late trips
mutex_destroy().

Check the queue liveness inside the queue lock, and clear queue->sock
under the same lock.  The teardown clears NVME_TCP_Q_LIVE under the
lock well before the socket is released, so a reader either sees the
bit cleared or a socket that cannot be released while it holds the
lock.  To also close the lock lifetime race, the queue locks are now
owned by the controller: they are initialized with the queue array and
only destroyed when the controller is freed, which cannot happen while
a sysfs attribute read is still in progress.  The queue count is
computed by the NVME_TCP_OPT_NR_QUEUES() macro from the original
connect options for both initialization and destruction, as reconnects
may shrink ctrl->queue_count.

items.title: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: f2fs: fix to avoid potential reference count leak i…
items.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

f2fs: fix to avoid potential reference count leak in do_garbage_collect()

In do_garbage_collect(), we have reserved reference counts on summary cache
of all segments, once gc_thread encounter freezing, we need to release all
reference counts.

items.title: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: arm64: vgic: Stop the target vcpu when disabli…
items.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: arm64: vgic: Stop the target vcpu when disabling LPIs

Disabling LPIs is pretty nasty, as it directly messes with the AP list
of the affected CPU, which could be running... This has the potential to
lead to really bad behaviours, and we should not be doing that.

Take example on the way the Active state is handled and simply pause the
the vcpu so that we are sure it is in a quiescent state, and the state be
safely manipulated.

Nobody has any expectation of performance for this anyway.

items.title: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: f2fs: bound the SIT/NAT bitmaps by the checkpoint p…
items.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

f2fs: bound the SIT/NAT bitmaps by the checkpoint pack

sit_ver_bitmap_bytesize and nat_ver_bitmap_bytesize are used as memcpy
lengths into and out of sbi->ckpt, which is sized from cp_payload alone,
and nothing compares either length against that allocation.

sanity_check_ckpt() has checked these two fields since c77ec61ca0a4, which
added them after a crafted image overran build_sit_info(). That check ties
each length to a segment count; it never compares either against the
allocation, which is the half this adds.

Mounting over-reads in build_sit_info() and build_node_manager(), and the
first checkpoint writes the same lengths back through the same pointers,
so the over-read's contents reach the on-disk checkpoint. An unmount is
enough; the filesystem does not have to be used.

Bound both ends the way __bitmap_ptr() lays them out. The three branches
differ, so a single sum of the two lengths would still admit a small
overflow when cp_payload is non-zero.

items.title: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: f2fs: return -EIO for a lost inode block after cp_e…
items.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

f2fs: return -EIO for a lost inode block after cp_error

After cp_error, dirty node caches are dropped without being written.
If such an inode was never written, its NAT entry is still NEW_ADDR,
and reading its inode block returns -ENOENT.

f2fs_get_dnode_of_data() passes that -ENOENT up, and callers take it
as a hole. Since the inode block is missing, the next offset can only
advance one block, so fiemap walks block by block up to maxbytes,
about 2^30 blocks, while holding the inode lock. It took hours in a
power-off recovery test after shutdown and blocked unlink and umount
on the file.

Return -EIO instead of -ENOENT when the inode block itself is missing
after cp_error or shutdown. A missing direct or indirect node is still
reported as -ENOENT.

items.title: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: f2fs: zone: fix to avoid bio split on sequential zo…
items.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

f2fs: zone: fix to avoid bio split on sequential zone

In the block layer, bio_split_to_limits() splits a bio if it exceeds
any underlying queue limits:
1. queue_max_sectors: Splits bios larger than the transfer limit. This
   limit is set by the device driver/DMA controller (max_hw_sectors) and
   device-mapper targets. When flushing dirty pages (governed by VFS
   writeback_chunk_size() and f2fs nr_pages_to_skip()), f2fs merges
   contiguous pages into bios up to 512KB (1024 sectors) or more without
   checking queue_max_sectors, which will be split if the device or DM
   target enforces a smaller limit.
2. queue_max_segments: Splits bios exceeding scatter-gather segment
   limits. f2fs allocates bios with up to 256 pages, exceeding the
   128-segment limit of DM targets (dm-default-key/dm-crypt) if pages
   are discontiguous.
3. chunk_sectors: Splits bios crossing chunk/zone boundaries. In f2fs,
   section_size strictly matches zone_size, and block allocation never
   spans across section boundaries, so bios never cross chunk_sectors.

Crucially, when bio_split_to_limits() splits a bio, bio_submit_split()
submits the tail half via submit_bio_noacct() before returning the head
half to the caller. On a sequential zoned device, this causes the tail
bio to arrive at the zone write plug before the head:

  dm-3: zone 7: prepare_bio wp mismatch: bio sector 30720 offset 2048
  != wp_offset 248, len 248

The write plug rejects the out-of-order tail with BLK_STS_IOERR, causing
f2fs_stop_checkpoint() and remounting the filesystem read-only:

items.title: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: wifi: rtw88: usb: bound what the driver feeds the a…
items.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

wifi: rtw88: usb: bound what the driver feeds the after-DTIM queue

Frames routed to the high queue are transmitted right after DTIM beacons
only, inside the ATIM window, while they wait in the shared TX page pool.
The driver puts no limit on how many it hands over, so as long as one
station dozes, any sustained broadcast or multicast traffic outruns the
drain and empties the pool: measured on an RTL8822BU AP with a single
client in power save and ~40 frames/s of mDNS chatter, the free page
count at 0x240 goes from 1803 to 16 in about 100 seconds and stays there
for as long as the traffic lasts. From that point every other transmit
queues behind the backlog, authentication responses arrive too late for
anyone to join, and the reserved page download fails ("error beacon
valid"). The AP keeps beaconing and only a reboot recovers.

Feed the high queue through a small budget that refills below the
measured drain rate (about 3 frames per DTIM, ~15/s at dtim_period 2 on
the default 2 TU ATIM window); whatever exceeds the budget leaves on its
access category queue right away. The high queue backlog is now bounded
by the burst size under any load, so the page pool cannot run dry, at
the price that a dozing station may miss part of a broadcast storm.

items.title: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: wifi: rtw88: usb: route bmc frames via the high que…
items.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

wifi: rtw88: usb: route bmc frames via the high queue only for DTIM delivery

In AP mode every broadcast and multicast data frame is routed to
TX_DESC_QSEL_HIGH, the after-DTIM queue, whether or not anybody is
asleep. The firmware drains that queue at beacon pace, a dozen or so
frames per second measured on RTL8822BU, while one associated client's
mDNS/SSDP chatter alone exceeds that. The excess accumulates inside
the chip until the shared TX page pool is exhausted (measured: 14 of
1803 pages left). From that point every host-sourced frame queues
behind the backlog: authentication responses reach the air seconds
after the client has given up, so no station can associate anymore,
and the beacon reserved-page download fails the BCN_VALID poll
("error beacon valid") because it needs pages from the same pool. The
AP keeps beaconing, so the failure looks like a silent RX stall and
only a reboot recovers.

mac80211 already decides when after-DTIM delivery is needed: it sets
IEEE80211_TX_CTL_SEND_AFTER_DTIM on bmc frames only while at least one
station is actually dozing. Honor that instead of routing
unconditionally: flagged frames keep going through the high queue with
the MORE_DATA and HGQMD handling introduced by commit 076f786a0ae1
("wifi: rtw88: Fix AP mode incorrect DTIM behavior"), everything else
leaves at line rate through the AC queues. This partially reverts the
usb.c hunk of that commit, whose unconditional routing is what lets
the backlog build up.

On a bench AP (USB2, 20 MHz, WPA2, hostapd, a Windows client driven
through disconnect/reconnect cycles): reconnects fail 0/5 on RTL8822BU
and 0/3 on RTL8821CU before this change, and pass 10/10 and 5/5 with
it, with the page pool staying healthy and no beacon errors logged.

items.title: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: assoc_array: keep gc's cleanup out of the live tree…
items.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

assoc_array: keep gc's cleanup out of the live tree on allocation failure

assoc_array_gc() builds a copy of the tree.  Where the copy reaches a
shortcut, it allocates the copy of the shortcut with kmalloc_flex(),
fills it with memcpy(), links it into the new tree, and only then
allocates the copy of the node after it.  The memcpy() leaves the new
shortcut's next_node pointing at the old tree's node, so if that second
allocation fails, the cleanup, assoc_array_destroy_subtree() on the new
tree, follows the new shortcut into the old tree, and the BUG_ON() on
the old node's back pointer fires.

Allocate the node first, and the shortcut once the node exists, freeing
the node again if the shortcut cannot be allocated.  A copied shortcut
is then only linked into the new tree when the copy of its node is there
to follow it.  Nothing else changes: with no allocation failing, the
trees gc builds are the same as before.

Found by a userspace test that makes each allocation of each operation
fail in turn.

items.title: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: assoc_array: don't chain a new shortcut onto an exi…
items.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

assoc_array: don't chain a new shortcut onto an existing one

When a full node's leaves and the new key all share the node's segment,
assoc_array_insert_into_terminal_node() replaces the node with a
shortcut to a pair of new nodes.  If the node is itself the target of a
shortcut, the new shortcut is installed as that shortcut's next node,
and a shortcut leading to a shortcut is something nothing expects:
assoc_array_walk() indexes the second one as a node, and
assoc_array_apply_edit() hits the BUG_ON() in the loop that adjusts
nr_leaves_on_branch, on that same insertion.

Deletion gets a node there.  When the subtree below a shortcut shrinks
enough, assoc_array_delete() collapses it into one node below the
shortcut, and the leaves it collects can all share that node's segment.
The next key that shares it too takes this path.  Eighteen insertions
and a deletion are enough: sixteen keys that agree on bits 0-11, one
that leaves them at bit 8 and is deleted again, and one more that agrees
with the sixteen.

Have the new shortcut replace the one in front of the node as well.
assoc_array_insert_shortcut() gives it that shortcut's back pointer and
parent slot, so the caller installs it where that one was, and excises
the old shortcut along with the node, which takes a second entry in
excised_meta[].  The new shortcut's index key comes from the new key up
to the new skip level, so it covers what the old one did.

Found by a userspace test doing random insertions and deletions on keys
that share long prefixes; a targeted case builds a shortcut, deletes
down to the collapse and inserts one more key.

items.title: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: iommufd/iova_bitmap: Ensure that iova_bitmap_set()…
items.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

iommufd/iova_bitmap: Ensure that iova_bitmap_set() handles the full IOVA

Generally userspace is going to step the dirty bitmap through the IOVA
space. However if the bitmap ends in the middle of a large PTE this is
problematic. The first step will clear the dirty bit and report dirty to
the end of its bitmap while the second step will see the clear'd dirty and
report clean for the start of the bitmap. If it happens this ends up
losing dirties.

Further this function is missing bounds checking so if this does happen
ther is a good chance it will write memory beyond what the userspace was
expecting.

Return an error code if this illegal condition happens.

items.title: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: f2fs: release a removed xattr node in roll-forward…
items.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

f2fs: release a removed xattr node in roll-forward recovery

When xattrs shrink enough to fit in the inline xattr area,
write_all_xattrs() truncates the xattr node and clears i_xattr_nid. If
the file is then fsynced without a checkpoint, only the inode block is
written, with i_xattr_nid of 0.

Roll-forward recovery starts from the checkpointed inode, whose
i_xattr_nid still points to the old xattr node.
f2fs_recover_inline_xattr() copies only the inline xattr area, and
f2fs_update_inode() writes the old i_xattr_nid back. So the inode keeps
the stale xattr node:

 - The node block is never released, and fsck reports "nonzero bytes in
   xattr space after end of list".
 - If the inline xattr list ends exactly at the end of the inline area,
   its terminator is read from the stale node, and the removed xattrs
   come back after recovery.

When the fsynced inode has no xattr node but the checkpointed one has,
release the old xattr node as truncate_node() does: check its block
address, invalidate the block and drop its node cache, which may still
be dirty.

items.title: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: f2fs: fix to invalidate curseg if change_curseg() f…
items.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

f2fs: fix to invalidate curseg if change_curseg() fails

Our consistency stress test (fsstress + fio + atomic write workers +
"f2fs_io shutdown 1") triggers below kernel BUG:

 F2FS-fs (vdd): Stopped filesystem due to reason: 0
 ------------[ cut here ]------------
 kernel BUG at fs/f2fs/segment.c:3989!
 Oops: invalid opcode: 0000 [#1] SMP KASAN PTI
 Workqueue: writeback wb_workfn (flush-253:48)
 RIP: 0010:f2fs_allocate_data_block+0x257a/0x38e0
 Call Trace:
  <TASK>
  do_write_block+0x155/0xc10
  f2fs_outplace_write_data+0x192/0x340
  f2fs_do_write_data_page+0xc57/0x1880
  f2fs_write_single_data_page+0xda9/0x15a0
  f2fs_write_cache_pages+0x973/0x1f20
  __f2fs_write_data_pages+0x6c4/0x1890
  do_writepages+0x21e/0x560
  __writeback_single_inode+0x119/0x11b0
  writeback_sb_inodes+0x67d/0x17a0
  wb_writeback+0x207/0x820
  wb_workfn+0x128/0xc30
  process_one_work+0x925/0x1600
  worker_thread+0x60a/0xff0
  kthread+0x35f/0x460
  ret_from_fork+0x474/0x7e0
  ret_from_fork_asm+0x1a/0x30
  </TASK>

The BUG is f2fs_bug_on(sbi, curseg->next_blkoff >= BLKS_PER_SEG(sbi))
in f2fs_allocate_data_block(), next_blkoff was 512.

The root cause is a race in between atomic write commit and shutdown
as below:

Thread A (commit atomic write)  Thread B (shutdown)        Thread C (writeback)
- f2fs_ioc_commit_atomic_write
 - f2fs_commit_atomic_write
  - __f2fs_commit_atomic_write
   - __replace_atomic_write_block
    - f2fs_replace_block
     - __f2fs_replace_block
                                - f2fs_ioc_shutdown
                                 - f2fs_do_shutdown
                                 : F2FS_GOING_DOWN_METASYNC
                                  - f2fs_sync_fs
                                                           - f2fs_write_single_data_page
                                                           : pass f2fs_cp_error() check
                                  - f2fs_stop_checkpoint
                                  : set CP_ERROR_FLAG
      - change_curseg
       - reset_curseg
       : curseg->segno = new_segno
       : curseg->alloc_type = SSR
       : curseg->next_blkoff = __next_free_blkoff()
         which is BLKS_PER_SEG if there is no free
         slot in new_segno
       - f2fs_get_sum_cache
       : return -EIO due to f2fs_cp_error()
      : return error w/o restoring curseg
     : goto out_unlock, skip restoring
       old segno, blkoff and alloc_type
                                                            - f2fs_do_write_data_page
                                                             - f2fs_outplace_write_data
                                                              - do_write_block
                                                               - f2fs_allocate_data_block
                                                               : curseg->segno is valid
                                                               : f2fs_bug_on(next_blkoff >=
                                                                 BLKS_PER_SEG)

Since commit 86f33603f8c5 ("f2fs: handle errors of
f2fs_get_meta_page_nofail"), change_curseg() can fail after the curseg
has already been switched to the new segment, then the curseg is left
in an inconsistent state: it points to a segment which may have no
free slot, its summary block is zeroed, and the caller can not restore
it. Subsequent block allocation on the curseg will trigger the BUG.
Moreover, the writeback thread dies with curseg_lock, curseg_mutex and
sentry_lock held, so the commit, shutdown and other I/O threads hang
in D state.

Since change_curseg() only fails once CP_ERROR_FLAG is set, no
checkpoint will be committed afterward, let's invalidate the curseg via
reset_curseg_fields() on failure, as new_curseg() does for -ENOSPC,
then f2fs_allocate_data_block() will fail with -ENOSPC on the curseg
instead of triggering BUG, and do_write_block() can handle the error
since CP_ERROR_FLA
---truncated---

items.title: A flaw was found in Keycloak.
items.description: A flaw was found in Keycloak. When a client application enforces step-up authentication or multi-factor authentication (MFA) via a minimum authentication level, Keycloak fails to apply this requirement to login sessions initiated through the credential reset endpoint. An attacker who possesses a user's initial credentials (such as a password) can navigate from the reset interface back to the standard login form and authenticate without completing the required second factor. This flaw allows an attacker to obtain valid access tokens and gain unauthorized access to protected services without satisfying mandatory security controls.

items.title: An uncontrolled recursion vulnerability exists in the LINE iOS app prior to version 26.19.0.
items.description:
An uncontrolled recursion vulnerability exists in the LINE iOS app prior to version 26.19.0.

The Flex Message processing component does not adequately validate the structure of externally supplied message content.

As a result, an attacker who is able to send a crafted message to a victim could cause the application to crash when the message is received or displayed.

A server-side mitigation has been deployed that also protects existing iOS clients that have not been updated to version 26.19.0.

items.title: A flaw was found in Keycloak.
items.description: A flaw was found in Keycloak. When an administrator revokes tokens by setting a not-before revocation cutoff, Keycloak fails to enforce this boundary when processing User-Managed Access (UMA) grant requests using ID token claims. An authenticated remote user with an active session can submit a previously revoked ID token to receive a fresh Requesting Party Token (RPT). This flaw allows an attacker to bypass token revocation and retain unauthorized access to protected resources.

items.title: A flaw was found in Keycloak.
items.description: A flaw was found in Keycloak. When processing token requests using the User-Managed Access (UMA) grant, Keycloak fails to verify whether a target client or resource server is enabled before issuing an authorization token. An authenticated remote user can exploit this flaw to obtain valid Requesting Party Tokens (RPTs) for disabled clients, bypassing administrative access controls and permissions restrictions.

items.title: A flaw was found in Keycloak.
items.description: A flaw was found in Keycloak. The Account API endpoint for sharing resources fails to verify whether owner-managed access is enabled and accepts permission scopes not assigned to the resource. An authenticated user can exploit this vulnerability to generate pre-granted permission tickets, causing Keycloak to bypass policy evaluation and issue access tokens with unauthorized scopes.

items.title: Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via unchecked exponent length in binary REAL decoding.
items.description:
Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via unchecked exponent length in binary REAL decoding.

Binary REAL decoding never bounds-checks the exponent length against the available content. For a minimal one-byte binary REAL, the exponent byte is read from outside the element, making the mantissa length -1. Perl reads a negative length as an offset from the end of the string, so the mantissa is nearly all of the input that follows the element. The long-form exponent path also omits the extra length octet when sizing the mantissa.

An attacker who controls the decoded data can exhaust CPU with a list of such values, as each mantissa loop iterates over the remaining input. The decoded values are also computed from bytes outside each element.

items.title: Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via exponent-notation string in INTEGER encoding.
items.description:
Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via exponent-notation string in INTEGER encoding.

The encoder routes any value with abs >= 2**31 to i2osp without validating that it is an integer. A string in exponent notation such as "1e8000" passes that threshold. Math::BigInt expands it to an 8001-digit integer, and i2osp's per-octet conversion loop is quadratic in that size.

An attacker who controls encoded INTEGER values can exhaust CPU with a short exponent-notation string.

items.title: Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via zero-length BIT STRING content.
items.description:
Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via zero-length BIT STRING content.

A BIT STRING with zero content octets passes -1 to substr as the length. Perl reads a negative length as an offset from the end of the string, so the decoded value is nearly all of the input that follows the element. In the constructed form each zero-length segment copies the rest of the input again, so memory grows with the square of the input size.

An attacker who controls the decoded data can exhaust memory with a short constructed BIT STRING. The resulting value also contains bytes from adjacent input.

items.title: Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via unlimited recursion depth in constructed-form s…
items.description:
Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via unlimited recursion depth in constructed-form string decoding.

Any constructed-form string element causes the decoder to recurse on the element's contents. The BER encoding controls nesting depth at four bytes per level, with no bound checked. Perl recursion is heap-allocated, so the process grows without a stack crash.

An attacker who controls the decoded data can exhaust memory with a small deeply nested constructed string.

items.title: Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via a declared element length passed unchecked to s…
items.description:
Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via a declared element length passed unchecked to sysread in asn_read and asn_get.

The length an element declares in its BER header is passed to sysread as the read size. Perl grows the target buffer to that size before reading, so memory is allocated from the declared length, not from the data received. A 6-byte header can declare a length of up to 4GB.

A single header makes the reading process allocate the declared size. Where the allocation fails, perl exits with "Out of memory", which eval cannot catch.

items.title: Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via unbounded arc length in OBJECT IDENTIFIER decoding…
items.description:
Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via unbounded arc length in OBJECT IDENTIFIER decoding and encoding.

The content of an OBJECT IDENTIFIER or RELATIVE-OID element is passed to unpack "w*" on decode, and the arcs of an OID string to pack "w*" on encode. Perl converts each arc to or from its decimal string in time quadratic in the arc's length, and nothing limits that length.

An attacker who controls the decoded data, or an OID string passed to encode, can exhaust CPU with a single oversized arc.

items.title: Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via quadratic bigint loop in os2ip.
items.description:
Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via quadratic bigint loop in os2ip.

Every INTEGER or ENUMERATED longer than four content octets reaches os2ip, which iterates over each content octet with $result = ($result * 256) + $octet. Each multiplication operates on a bigint that grows by one octet per step, so decoding an n-octet value takes O(n^2) bigint work. Nothing limits content length before this loop runs.

An attacker who controls the decoded data can exhaust CPU with a single oversized INTEGER or ENUMERATED value.

items.title: Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via unbounded MSG_PEEK buffer doubling in asn_recv.
items.description:
Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via unbounded MSG_PEEK buffer doubling in asn_recv.

asn_recv peeks the socket in a loop, doubling the buffer size on each pass until a tag and length can be decoded. An inverted boolean guard ($tb || rather than $tb &&) prevents the need-more-data exit from firing once a tag byte has been decoded. When asn_decode_length returns no value because the length is absent or incomplete, no exit fires for that case either. MSG_PEEK leaves socket data unconsumed, so each re-peek returns at once while the buffer size doubles.

A single truncated BER header sent to a process calling asn_recv doubles the peek buffer until memory is exhausted. Perl's realloc failure is fatal and not catchable with eval.

items.title: Refitter allows arbitrary code execution through unescaped OpenAPI content-type values
items.description:
### Summary

Refitter emits the spec's content-type key (content map key in requestBody/responses) verbatim into a Refit `[Headers("Accept: <ct>", "Content-Type: <ct>")]` attribute string without escaping
`"`. A crafted value survives Refitter's default OpenAPI validation, breaks out of the attribute and
the enclosing interface + namespace, injects a top-level `file class` with a `[ModuleInitializer]`
method, and reopens so the file stays valid. .NET runs `[ModuleInitializer]` methods at assembly
load, so the attacker's code executes at application startup. Verified on Refitter 2.0.0 / .NET 8.

The malicious input is a content-type KEY such as: content: { 'application/<breakout>': {schema} }.
No `--skip-validation` is required.

### PoC

`reproduce.sh` (+ `make_spec.py`) attached: generates with default validation, compiles into a
console app, runs it (Main does not touch the client), and shows a marker written at assembly load.

### Impact

Code execution at assembly load (process startup) in any application that compiles a Refitter client
generated from an attacker-controlled or attacker-influenced OpenAPI description. Estimated Critical, e.g.
`CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N` (the CNA sets the final score).

### Suggested fix

Escape every spec-derived string before emitting it into a Refit attribute (escape `"`, `\`,
reject newlines) and validate characters. We recommend auditing all attribute emissions that embed
spec-derived values, using one shared encoder.
[reproduce.sh](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29394848/reproduce.sh)
[maintainer-report.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29394851/maintainer-report.txt)
[make_spec.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29394853/make_spec.py)

items.title: Refitter allows code execution through unescaped OpenAPI header parameter names
items.description:
### Summary

Refitter emits the spec's header parameter name (parameters[].name with in: header) verbatim into a Refit `[Header("<name>")]` attribute string without escaping
`"`. A crafted value survives Refitter's default OpenAPI validation, breaks out of the attribute and

The malicious input is a header parameter name. No `--skip-validation` is required. The query

### Impact

### Suggested fix

Escape every spec-derived string before emitting it into a Refit attribute (escape `"`, `\`,
reject newlines) and validate characters. We recommend auditing all attribute emissions that embed

items.title: Refitter allows arbitrary code execution through unescaped OpenAPI paths
items.description:
### Summary

Refitter emits each OpenAPI path (the paths-object key) verbatim into a Refit `[Get("<path>")]`
attribute string, without escaping `"` or restricting characters. A crafted single-line, /-prefixed
path survives Refitter's default OpenAPI validation yet closes the attribute string and the enclosing
interface + namespace, injects a top-level `file class` with a `[ModuleInitializer]` method, and
reopens a namespace + interface so the file stays valid. .NET runs `[ModuleInitializer]` methods when
the generated assembly is loaded, so the attacker's code executes at application startup. Verified on
Refitter 2.0.0 / .NET 8.

### Details

```
[Get("/p")] Task<string> Dummy(); } }
file class Evil { [System.Runtime.CompilerServices.ModuleInitializer]
  internal static void Init(){ /* attacker code */ } }
namespace N2 { public partial interface I2 { [Get("/q")]
        Task<string> GetU(string id);
    }
}
```

No `--skip-validation` is needed (the payload is a valid single-line path). The generated `.cs` is
compiled into the victim application; the module initializer runs at assembly load. This is distinct
from the value sinks (enum/default), which are escaped; the path sink has no escaping. The
`[Header("<name>")]` attribute is likewise emitted raw (header parameter names), at minimum a
build-breaking DoS.

### PoC

`reproduce.sh` (+ `make_spec.py`) attached: generates with default validation, compiles into a console
app, runs it (Main does not touch the client), and shows a marker written at assembly load. Verified
on 2.0.0.

### Impact

Code execution at assembly load (process startup) in any application that compiles a Refitter client
generated from an attacker-controlled or attacker-influenced OpenAPI description.

### Suggested fix

Escape the route template before emitting it into `[Get("…")]` (escape `"`, `\`, reject newlines) and
validate that paths contain only legal URI-template characters. Apply the same encoding to
`[Header(…)]`, `[Post/Put/Delete(…)]`, and every attribute that embeds a spec-derived string.
[maintainer-report.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29395228/maintainer-report.txt)
[make_spec.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29395229/make_spec.py)
[reproduce.sh](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29395230/reproduce.sh)

items.title: NATS Server: MQTT-over-WebSocket Path Can Crash WebSocket-Only JetStream Servers Before MQTT Is Enabled
items.description:
### Background

NATS.io is a high performance open source pub-sub distributed communication technology, built for the cloud, on-premise, IoT and edge computing.

The NATS Server can accept client connections over WebSocket and can also support MQTT over WebSocket when MQTT is configured.

### Problem Description

A WebSocket listener could route requests for the MQTT-over-WebSocket path into MQTT handling even when MQTT was not configured.

On affected deployments, an unauthenticated client with access to the WebSocket listener could reach uninitialized MQTT state and crash the server process.

This affects deployments that enable WebSocket while leaving MQTT disabled. Deployments where MQTT is intentionally configured initialize the MQTT state and are not affected in the same way.

### Affected Versions

Versions v2.14.2, v2.12.11 and below are vulnerable. The issue is fixed in v2.14.3 and v2.12.12.

### Workarounds

Deployments not using WebSocket are not affected. Deployments using both WebSockets and MQTT are not affected. No known workaround for deployments that need WebSocket without MQTT-over-WebSocket. Upgrade to a fixed release.

### References

 * GHSA advisory: <https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server/security/advisories/GHSA-p957-7v2w-g93g>
 * Credit: Vasco Franco, Trail of Bits

items.title: NATS Server allows unauthenticated memory exhaustion through incomplete MQTT CONNECT packets
items.description:
### Background

NATS.io is a high performance open source pub-sub distributed communication technology, built for the cloud, on-premise, IoT and edge computing.

The NATS Server supports MQTT clients, including authentication and parsing of MQTT `CONNECT` packets.

### Problem Description

An unauthenticated MQTT client could cause the server to retain large incomplete MQTT `CONNECT` packets before authentication completed.

The parser retained partial pre-authentication packet data while waiting for the advertised MQTT packet length to be completed. An attacker could therefore consume server memory until authentication timeouts closed the connections.

### Affected Versions

Versions v2.14.2, v2.12.11 and below are vulnerable. The issue is fixed in v2.14.3 and v2.12.12.

### Workarounds

Deployments not using MQTT are not affected. Deployments that need MQTT should upgrade to a fixed release.

### References

 * GHSA advisory: <https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server/security/advisories/GHSA-r72h-j7qq-v6qg>
 * Credit: Asritha Bodepudi, Trail of Bits

items.title: NATS Server MQTT retained messages and QoS replay bypass subscription deny rules
items.description:
### Background

NATS.io is a high performance open source pub-sub distributed communication technology, built for the cloud, on-premise, IoT and edge computing.

The NATS Server MQTT support includes retained messages and QoS1+ durable delivery. NATS subscription permissions can allow broad wildcard subscriptions while denying more sensitive subjects.

### Problem Description

MQTT retained message delivery and QoS1+ durable replay could deliver messages whose original topics matched a subscriber's configured subscribe deny rules.

Normal live delivery applied the delivery-time deny check. These MQTT delivery paths did not consistently recheck the concrete original topic before sending the MQTT `PUBLISH` to the subscriber.

The issue affects MQTT subscribers with broad wildcard subscribe permissions where more specific topics are denied. Normal live delivery can be blocked while retained or replayed delivery still sends the denied topic.

### Affected Versions

Versions v2.14.2, v2.12.11 and below are vulnerable. The issue is fixed in v2.14.3 and v2.12.12.

### Workarounds

No known workaround for deployments that require MQTT. Upgrade to a fixed release. Deployments not using MQTT are not affected.

### References

 * GHSA advisory: <https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server/security/advisories/GHSA-7qmq-8cc4-hxwg>
 * Credit: Asritha Bodepudi, Trail of Bits

items.title: snark-verifier: Halo 2 aggregation circuit mishandles point-at-infinity proof elements
items.description:
### Summary
The Halo 2 aggregation circuit could mishandle proof elements encoded as the point at infinity.

When an assigned proof point appeared in an MSM term with constant scalar one, the Halo 2 loader used a scalar-one shortcut that passed the assigned point directly into the EC sum helper. The EC sum implementation used by that path assumed its inputs were non-identity points, while assigned proof points could represent the encoded identity `(0, 0)`.

### Details
`EcPointLoader::multi_scalar_multiplication` partitions MSM terms by scalar and base type. For `(Value::Constant(ONE), Value::Assigned(_))`, the loader placed the assigned base into the non-scaled variable-base list and later passed those points to `sum_with_const`.

The default Halo 2 shim delegates `sum_with_const` to halo2-lib `EccChip::sum`. In affected versions, that sum helper used incomplete affine addition and assumed that every input point was non-identity. A prover-controlled proof point encoded as `(0, 0)` could therefore enter the final aggregation sum through the scalar-one shortcut and affect the MSM or accumulator computation.

The issue was fixed in halo2-lib by updating `EccChip::sum` to treat encoded identity inputs as no-ops and to return `(0, 0)` when the total sum is the identity. This removes the non-identity input precondition from callers such as the Halo 2 aggregation loader.

### Impact
Recursive aggregation circuits using the Halo 2 loader could compute an MSM or accumulator with an identity proof element in a path whose implementation assumed non-identity inputs. This breaks the expected handling of point-at-infinity proof elements in aggregation.

Practical exploitability depends on the surrounding aggregation and final-decider checks, so this is rated medium severity.

items.title: Apache Roller: Apache Roller Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability
items.description:
Deserialization of Untrusted Data in Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code. The XML-RPC endpoint accepts vendor extension types and deserializes them before authenticating the requester.

This is the same vulnerability as CVE-2026-82384, which listed only Apache Roller 6.1.5 as affected. This issue is being actively exploited.

Users are recommended to upgrade to Apache Roller 6.1.6 or later, which disables the extension types and rejects XML-RPC requests when the XML-RPC feature is disabled.

Users who cannot upgrade right away should set "enabledForExtensions" to "false" in WEB-INF/web.xml, or remove the "/roller-services/xmlrpc" servlet mapping, and restart Roller. Disabling XML-RPC in the administration UI is not enough, because older versions deserialize the request before checking that setting.

items.description: Cisco Expressway Series contains a use of hard-coded credentials vulnerability that allows an unauthenticated, remote attacker with persistent cookies and network access to execute commands as root on a clustered device via the database service.
items.kev_action: Apply mitigations in accordance with vendor instructions, ensuring compliance with CISA’s BOD 26-04 Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk (see URL in Notes) guidance and CISA’s “Forensics Triage Requirements” (see URL in Notes). Follow applicable BOD 26-04 guidance for cloud services or discontinue use of the product if mitigations are unavailable. Stakeholders are responsible for evaluating each asset's internet exposure and ensuring adherence to BOD 26-04 patching guidelines.

items.title: A flaw was found in Keycloak.
items.description: A flaw was found in Keycloak. When configured with a database that uses case-insensitive collation, Keycloak resolves realm URLs regardless of letter casing. A remote attacker can exploit this behavior by sending requests with alternate letter casing to bypass upstream reverse proxy access controls that rely on case-sensitive path matching. This issue can expose restricted authentication endpoints intended only for internal access, though Keycloak's internal authentication mechanisms remain intact.

items.title: Flyto2 Core: Arbitrary file write via unguarded data.*/file.* modules (incomplete fix of CVE-2026-67429)
items.description: Flyto2 Core is an execution kernel for automation and AI-agent workflows. Prior to 2.26.8, the earlier CVE-2026-67429 remediation applied validate_path_with_env_config() to only a hand-picked set of file-writing modules, leaving data.csv.write in src/core/modules/atomic/data/csv_write.py, data.json_to_csv in src/core/modules/atomic/data/json_to_csv.py, file.copy in src/core/modules/atomic/file/copy.py, and file.move in src/core/modules/atomic/file/move.py outside the FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR confinement boundary. The advisory also identifies unguarded modules across the broader data.*, file.*, and report-writer families. data.csv.write relies on a .. substring denylist that does not reject absolute paths, while the other named modules accept caller-controlled output or destination paths without the canonical guard. A caller able to execute modules or recipes can therefore write attacker-controlled content outside the configured sandbox, potentially overwriting application code, recipes, startup files, scheduled-task files, or authorization files and gaining code execution on the host. This issue is fixed in version 2.26.8.

items.title: Flyto2 Core: http.paginate follows server-supplied next-page URLs (Link header / cursor) without SSRF revalidation
items.description: Flyto2 Core is an execution kernel for automation and AI-agent workflows. Prior to 2.26.8, http.paginate in src/core/modules/atomic/http/paginate.py validates only the initial base_url, and _paginate_link_header then follows a server-supplied Link: rel="next" URL without calling the SSRF guard again. A low-privileged caller can make an allowed first page point the next request at an internal or metadata service, causing a readable second-order SSRF whose response body is aggregated into all_items and returned. This issue is fixed in version 2.26.8.

items.title: Flyto2 Core: SSRF guard validates the resolved IP but connects by hostname, allowing DNS-rebinding TOCTOU
items.description: Flyto2 Core is an execution kernel for automation and AI-agent workflows. Prior to 2.26.8, validate_url_ssrf in src/core/utils.py resolves and checks a hostname but returns the hostname URL rather than the validated address, and session.get in http.get performs an independent DNS lookup when connecting. A low-privileged caller with control of the hostname's DNS can make the first lookup return a public address and the connection-time lookup return an internal address, bypassing the SSRF guard for all modules that call it and exposing readable internal or metadata-service responses. Successful exploitation requires attacker-controlled DNS and a successful timing-dependent answer change between the two lookups. This issue is fixed in version 2.26.8.

items.title: Flyto2 Core: SSRF guard bypass via DNS rebinding (validate_url_ssrf resolves-then-connects without pinning)
items.description: Flyto2 Core is an execution kernel for automation and AI-agent workflows. Prior to 2.26.8, validate_url_ssrf() in src/core/utils.py validates one DNS answer and then returns the hostname, while guarded_aiohttp_request(), enforce_outbound_url(), and validate_url_with_env_config() allow the outbound connection to perform an independent second lookup. A caller with control of the hostname's DNS can make validation see a public address and make the connection see an internal address, bypassing the guard across its outbound consumers and exposing readable internal or metadata-service responses. The attack requires low or zero DNS TTL behavior and a successful timing-dependent answer change; static multiple-address answers are checked and do not provide the same bypass. This issue is fixed in version 2.26.8.

items.title: Flyto2 Core is an execution kernel for automation and AI-agent workflows.
items.description: Flyto2 Core is an execution kernel for automation and AI-agent workflows. Prior to 2.26.8, the MCP run_recipe tool in src/core/mcp_handler.py accepts a caller-controlled recipe_name that load_recipe() in src/cli/recipe.py appends to the src/recipes path without resolved-path containment. Parent-directory segments can therefore make Flyto load and execute a YAML workflow outside the bundled recipe directory, bypassing the boundary represented by list_recipes(). This does not necessarily provide unrestricted code execution because available workflow modules remain subject to Flyto's module policy, but it permits unintended execution of allowed browser, network, file, and data-processing modules. This issue is fixed in version 2.26.8.

items.title: netty-incubator-codec-ohttp: OHTTP codecs retain consumed outer cumulation buffers after completed exchanges
items.description: netty-incubator-codec-ohttp implements Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP) gateway and client functionality using Netty. From 0.0.20.Final until 0.0.27.Final, OHttpClientCodec in codec-ohttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpClientCodec.java and OHttpServerCodec in codec-ohttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpServerCodec.java retain the consumed outer cumulationBuffer after a valid OHTTP exchange completes, even though OHttpRequestResponseContext.destroy in codec-ohttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpRequestResponseContext.java releases the inner Binary HTTP cumulation and the channel remains active. A peer can complete a large request or response and leave the keep-alive connection idle, causing the client and server handlers to retain the current high-water pooled or direct buffer capacity until later inbound content replaces it or the handler is removed. Many long-lived idle connections can pin substantial memory and create availability pressure. The issue does not cause unbounded growth for repeated exchanges on a single channel. This issue is fixed in version 0.0.27.Final.

items.title: netty-incubator-codec-ohttp implements Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP) gateway and client functionality using Netty.
items.description: netty-incubator-codec-ohttp implements Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP) gateway and client functionality using Netty. Prior to 0.0.23.Final, BinaryHttpParser.readFieldLine in codec-bhttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/bhttp/BinaryHttpParser.java treats a complete field line that ends exactly at a known field-section boundary as incomplete and returns without consuming bytes. BinaryHttpParser.readFieldSection then leaves fieldSectionLength unchanged and repeats the loop because its forward-progress checks are Java assertions, which are normally disabled in production. A remote peer that sends a known-length Binary HTTP header or trailer section ending at that boundary can make the parser spin indefinitely and pin the Netty event-loop or worker thread responsible for the channel. This issue is fixed in version 0.0.23.Final.

items.title: netty-incubator-codec-ohttp implements Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP) gateway and client functionality using Netty.
items.description: netty-incubator-codec-ohttp implements Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP) gateway and client functionality using Netty. Prior to 0.0.23.Final, BinaryHttpParser.readFieldSection in codec-bhttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/bhttp/BinaryHttpParser.java loops while fieldSectionLength is nonzero and relies on disabled-by-default assertions to require BinaryHttpParser.readFieldLine to return a value and consume bytes. A corrupt field line can consume more bytes than its understated declared section length and drive the counter negative, or a truncated field line can return without consuming data and leave the parser in the same state. An unauthenticated OHTTP peer can encrypt such Binary HTTP content under the gateway public configuration, reach OHttpRequestResponseContext.ContentDecoder.decodeChunk, and permanently pin a Netty event-loop thread at full CPU before application business logic. Multiple requests can exhaust the event-loop group and deny service until restart. This issue is fixed in version 0.0.23.Final.

items.title: netty-incubator-codec-ohttp implements Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP) gateway and client functionality using Netty.
items.description: netty-incubator-codec-ohttp implements Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP) gateway and client functionality using Netty. Prior to 0.0.23.Final, BinaryHttpParser does not enforce limits on encoded variable-length fields controlled by a remote peer. A remote peer can cause the decoder to buffer data indefinitely until memory is exhausted, causing denial of service. This issue is fixed in version 0.0.23.Final.

items.title: netty-incubator-codec-ohttp implements Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP) gateway and client functionality using Netty.
items.description: netty-incubator-codec-ohttp implements Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP) gateway and client functionality using Netty. Prior to 0.0.23.Final, BoringSSLAsymmetricCipherKeyPair.toString in codec-ohttp-hpke-classes-boringssl/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/hpke/boringssl/BoringSSLAsymmetricCipherKeyPair.java includes its private parameter, BoringSSLAsymmetricKeyParameter.toString in codec-ohttp-hpke-classes-boringssl/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/hpke/boringssl/BoringSSLAsymmetricKeyParameter.java renders the complete private-key byte array when isPrivate is true, and BoringSSL.EVP_HPKE_KEY_init_or_throw in codec-ohttp-hpke-classes-boringssl/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/hpke/boringssl/BoringSSL.java includes rejected privateKeyBytes in an exception message. Applications that log affected key-pair objects or initialization exceptions can persist complete HPKE private key material in logs or telemetry. Anyone who can read those records can recover the key and may compromise OHTTP message confidentiality or authenticity expectations while the key remains usable. This issue is fixed in version 0.0.23.Final.

items.title: netty-incubator-codec-ohttp implements Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP) gateway and client functionality using Netty.
items.description: netty-incubator-codec-ohttp implements Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP) gateway and client functionality using Netty. Prior to 0.0.23.Final, BinaryHttpParser in codec-bhttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/bhttp/BinaryHttpParser.java accumulates attacker-controlled Binary HTTP variable-length integers into the int offset sumBytes. BinaryHttpParser.readRequestHead, BinaryHttpParser.readFieldLine, and BinaryHttpParser.getIndeterminateLength can narrow long lengths into that offset, causing integer wraparound before buffer indices are calculated. A remote peer that supplies a valid large encoded length to BinaryHttpParser or BinaryHttpDecoder can trigger an unchecked bounds exception from a small malformed message, fail or close the channel, and repeatedly cause denial of service. Java and Netty bounds checks prevent memory corruption, and no information disclosure was observed. This issue is fixed in version 0.0.23.Final.

items.title: In Dolibarr before 24.0.3, dolForgeSQLCriteriaCallback() in htdocs/core/lib/functions.lib.php allows account takeover b…
items.description: In Dolibarr before 24.0.3, dolForgeSQLCriteriaCallback() in htdocs/core/lib/functions.lib.php allows account takeover because it strips only a single table-name prefix from a Universal Search Filter (sqlfilters) operand before checking it against the forbidden-field denylist (pass, pass_crypted, api_key). MariaDB and MySQL accept a two-level qualification such as schema.alias.column, so an operand of the form dolibarr.u.pass_crypted survives the check and is emitted into the WHERE clause. A remote authenticated user holding only the holiday read and readall permissions, which confer no user-management or administrative access, can use the resulting boolean oracle at GET /api/index.php/holidays to recover any user's bcrypt password hash and api_key one character at a time, including an administrator's. Because api_key is accepted directly by the REST API as a bearer credential, this yields full administrative control of the application. This bypasses the fix for CVE-2026-89012, which added only a strtolower() call and did not address prefix depth. The same denylist also omits pass_temp, which stores a password in cleartext, as well as national_registration_number, salary, birth, address, personal_mobile and note_private.

items.title: A flaw was found in Keycloak.
items.description: A flaw was found in Keycloak. This vulnerability allows an authenticated remote attacker to cause a denial of service by terminating active sessions of arbitrary users. When processing Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) documents that lack a root signature, Keycloak accepts the request as long as any assertion within the document is signed, without verifying its context or placement. An attacker holding a validly signed assertion can embed it into an unsigned logout request for another user, causing Keycloak to accept the forged request and terminate the victim's session.

items.title: Etherpad: Pre-auth arbitrary file read
items.description: Etherpad is a real-time collaborative editor. From 1.8.14 until 3.3.3, the pre-authentication /static/* plugin asset handler in src/node/utils/Minify.ts performs a backslash-to-forward-slash conversion after src/node/utils/sanitizePathname.ts has completed its POSIX path checks. On POSIX systems the sanitizer correctly treats backslashes as ordinary filename bytes, but the later conversion turns encoded backslash-separated parent-directory segments into traversal components without revalidation or containment. The expressPreSession registration and the always-present ep_etherpad-lite core pseudo-plugin make this path reachable without credentials, allowing a remote attacker to read any file available to the Etherpad process. Disclosed configuration or environment secrets can expose administrator credentials, after which the administrator plugin installer can provide in-process code execution and full server compromise. This issue is fixed in version 3.3.3.

items.title: Safari MCP: JavaScript injection through single-quoted tool arguments (backslash not escaped)
items.description:
### Impact

Sixteen places in `safari.js` placed a tool argument inside a single-quoted JavaScript string literal and escaped the single quote without first escaping backslashes. An argument containing a backslash followed by a quote therefore closed the literal, and the rest of the argument ran as JavaScript in the page.

Seven of the affected arguments belong to read-only tools that are exempt from the tab-ownership check: `filter` in `safari_network_details` and `safari_extract_links`, `level` in `safari_console_filter`, `selector` in `safari_snapshot`, `safari_accessibility_snapshot` and `safari_extract_tables`, and `dbName` / `storeName` in `safari_get_indexed_db`. An MCP client limited to read-only tools (with `safari_evaluate` and `safari_run_script` excluded from its allowlist) could still run arbitrary page JavaScript through them, including in a tab the session does not own. The other affected arguments are `ref` in `safari_select_option`, `safari_react_select_set` and `safari_react_select_list_options`, the key in `safari_press_key`, the file name in `safari_upload_file` and `safari_paste_image`, and the first line of the text in `safari_replace_editor`.

### Patches

Fixed in 2.22.15: every affected site uses the shared `escJsSingleQuote`, which escapes the backslash before the quote, and a test fails the build if a quote-only escape returns.

### Workarounds

Upgrade to 2.22.15. There is no configuration workaround: excluding `safari_evaluate` and `safari_run_script` from a client's tool list did not prevent the injection.

### Credits

Reported privately on 2026-10-09 by Aliaksandr Palei (@fakepooh) under the coordinated-disclosure process in SECURITY.md.

items.title: baserCMS: Path Traversal Bypass via realpath() in BcThemeFileService (CVE-2026-30940 Patch Bypass)
items.description: baserCMS is a website development framework. From 5.2.3 until 5.3.0, BcThemeFileService::getFullpath() in plugins/bc-theme-file/src/Service/BcThemeFileService.php skips its path containment check when realpath() fails for a nonexistent theme subdirectory selected by the type parameter. An authenticated administrator can supply a traversal path through the theme-file API to access locations outside the theme directory. The bypass of the CVE-2026-30940 fix can permit file writes, overwrites or deletion within the PHP process permissions and, where executable PHP can be written, remote code execution. This issue is fixed in 5.3.0.

items.title: baserCMS administrative API authorization bypass through session fallback
items.description: baserCMS is a website development framework. Prior to 5.3.0, getAuthenticationService permits an Api/Admin session authentication fallback based on the Referer header, although operator accounts have an Admin auth prefix and cannot obtain an Api/Admin JWT. An authenticated operator can therefore access /baser/api/admin/ endpoints whose permission.php entries have auth => true, including /baser/api/admin/baser-core/site_configs/view.json, even when the corresponding administrative functionality is restricted. This can disclose administrator-restricted configuration information. This issue is fixed in 5.3.0.

items.title: Reposilite is lightweight and easy-to-use repository management software dedicated to Maven-based artifacts in the JVM…
items.description: Reposilite is lightweight and easy-to-use repository management software dedicated to Maven-based artifacts in the JVM ecosystem. From 3.5.16 until 3.6.0, as stated by the advisory, the Maven directory-index page interpolates the request URI without HTML escaping in its title, heading, base URL, and parent-directory link. The advisory says the content-embedded ctx.uri() is percent-encoded, preventing tag injection, but that a single quote passes through and breaks the quoted Parent-Directory link; it also says Location.of strips single quotes, so the reachability of the described quote-based trigger remains unresolved. The listing shares the Admin UI origin and does not set the sandbox Content-Security-Policy used for artifact and Javadoc responses, so the reported script execution could access a user's local-storage token. A manager token could enable full instance compromise. The advisory reports version 3.6.0 as fixed.
