items.title: An unauthenticated SQL injection can occur on the front end of any site that uses craft.search to perform a search, all…
items.description:
An unauthenticated SQL injection can occur on the front end of any site that uses craft.search to perform a search, allowing stacked query execution and enabling escalation to an administrator.



Note that this only affects MySQL/MariaDB.

Impact  *  SQL injection — The attribute parameter is concatenated into the query unsanitized, and because PDO runs with emulated prepares, stacked statements execute. This gives unauthenticated read and write access to the application database.
  *  Privilege escalation to administrator — The write primitive was used to set the admin flag on user ID 1 in the users table, confirmed by reading the value back. Craft short-circuits its permission checks on this single column, so no further changes were needed. The same primitive can overwrite any account’s password hash.




Update to the patched versions (4.18.9 and 5.11.2) to get the fix.



If you cannot update immediately, you can block front-end requests with %5Battribute%5D and [attribute] anywhere in the query string as a temporary mitigation.

items.title: Claude Code: TOCTOU Race in Edit Tool Allows File Writes Outside the Workspace
items.description:
Claude Code validated Edit tool targets using point-in-time pathname and symlink resolution that was not bound to the underlying directory inodes or file descriptors. On macOS, a process running inside Claude Code's Bash sandbox could exploit the resulting time-of-check to time-of-use window by atomically swapping an in-workspace parent directory with a symlink after validation completed, causing the unsandboxed Edit implementation to overwrite an attacker-selected user-writable file outside the workspace. Exploiting this required the ability to run attacker-controlled code inside the sandbox, such as through a malicious repository or dependency script.

Users on standard Claude Code auto-update have received this fix automatically. Users performing manual updates are advised to update to the latest version.

Claude Code thanks hackerone.com/mahoraga007 (Sunder Singh) for reporting this issue.

items.title: croc: Overwrite-confirmation bypass via a crafted "croc-stdin-" filename on receive
items.description:
## Summary

croc is an end-to-end encrypted peer-to-peer file transfer tool. On the receiving side, the confirmation that normally protects an existing file from being overwritten or resumed is skipped whenever the received file's name starts with `croc-stdin-`, regardless of whether the incoming transfer is actually a text transfer. A sender can therefore name a file `croc-stdin-<existing-name>` and silently overwrite, truncate, or replace an existing file of that name in the receiver's working directory - including removing the existing file and substituting a symlink - without the `Overwrite?` prompt that the standard path requires. The exemption was introduced to keep croc's internal text-transfer artifacts from triggering prompts, but it is keyed on the filename prefix rather than on the transfer type, so any ordinary file transfer can claim the exemption.

## Vulnerability Details

Affected code at commit `b6f27da9401f2c3647c1adb6b77a46bb8c0923d2` (HEAD, v11.5.1+1):

The receive-side file-readiness loop in `src/croc/croc.go` decides whether to prompt before overwriting or resuming an existing destination file. The decision is made around line 3413:

```go
isStdinName := strings.HasPrefix(path.Base(fileInfo.Name), "croc-stdin-")
...
if destinationExists && !c.Options.Overwrite && !c.Options.Rename && !isStdinName {
    resumable := fileInfo.Size > 0 && fileInfo.Symlink == "" && recipientFileInfo.Mode().IsRegular()
    overwrite, promptErr := askReceiveOverwrite(c.clientContext(), fileInfo, resumable)
    if promptErr != nil {
        return promptErr
    }
    if !overwrite {
        continue
    }
}
```

`isStdinName` is derived purely from the received file's basename. The prompt is suppressed for any such name, even when `c.Options.SendingText` is false and the transfer is an ordinary file transfer whose name the sender chose.

When the prompt is skipped and the transfer declares `fileInfo.Size == 0` or a symlink (`fileInfo.Symlink != ""`), the loop calls `createEmptyFileAndFinish()` (src/croc/croc.go:3245), which - before creating the new entry - removes any existing file at the destination:

```go
if fileInfo.Symlink != "" {
    if err = validateReceiveSymlinkTarget(fileInfo.FolderRemote, fileInfo.Symlink); err != nil {
        return
    }
    log.Debug("creating symlink")
    // remove symlink if it exists
    if _, errExists := root.Lstat(pathToFile); errExists == nil {
        if err = root.Remove(pathToFile); err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }
    err = root.Symlink(fileInfo.Symlink, pathToFile)
    ...
}
```

For a normal (non-`croc-stdin-`) name, the overwrite prompt runs first, so the remove/replace step only happens with the user's explicit `y`. For a `croc-stdin-` name the entire prompt is bypassed: an existing `croc-stdin-*` file is deleted and replaced with the attacker's symlink (or, for `Size == 0`, truncated to an empty file) with no confirmation.

For a non-empty regular-file transfer with a `croc-stdin-` name, the same missing prompt lets the receive path proceed through `recipientInitializeFile()` (src/croc/croc.go:3109; the `os.O_RDWR` open is at 3136-3138): the existing file is opened `O_RDWR` (no `O_EXCL`), truncated to the sender-declared size when the sizes differ, and the sender's chunks are written at the declared offsets - a silent overwrite of the existing file's content.

Why the check is missing: the exemption was added deliberately so that croc's own `croc-stdin-*` text artifacts (created by `os.CreateTemp(".", "croc-stdin-")` for `croc send --text` / piped stdin) do not trigger an overwrite question every time. History: commit b687778d "bug fix: doesn't ask overwrite text Fixes #384" (2021-04-29) introduced the prefix-based skip, keyed on the filename and not on the transfer's `SendingText` flag. The branch that handles `Size == 0 || Symlink != ""` via `createEmptyFileAndFinish()` predates that (6386e4a8, 2019) and at the time ran unconditionally for every received name; the refactor 615af377 "fix: gate overwrites and receive hash algorithms" (2026-08-29, first released in v11.3.6) moved it below the overwrite-prompt gate, so after v11.3.6 the empty-file/symlink replacement reaches the remove-and-replace step without user confirmation only through the `croc-stdin-` exemption. The refactor extracted the prefix test into `isStdinName` and kept it filename-only, dropping the explicit `!c.Options.SendingText` conjunct that the pre-refactor prompt conditions still carried (615af377~1); the original intent was to suppress the prompt only for transfers actually marked as text. Because the exemption is keyed on a filename prefix the sender fully controls, any peer a user receives from can claim it.

The same prefix exemption also suppresses the `--rename` side of the decision (`if destinationExists && !isStdinName && c.Options.Rename`), so `--rename` receivers silently keep the attacker-chosen name and overwrite too.

This is distinct from the previously reported `croc-marked-files.txt` arbitrary file deletion (oss-sec 2026/Q3 #497, fixed in 11.0.3 by commit c0d51f0, which removed the on-disk cleanup list). That defect reached deletion through `RemoveMarkedFiles()`; this one reaches silent overwrite/replacement through the filename-keyed prompt exemption in the receive loop, which the 11.0.3 fix did not touch and which remains live at HEAD.

## Impact

An attacker who can send a file to a victim (croc's sender-is-untrusted model; the receiver accepts a transfer from them) can silently overwrite, truncate, or delete-and-replace an existing `croc-stdin-*` file in the receiver's working directory without the confirmation every other received name triggers. The attack needs the colliding file to already exist with an exact name the sender can predict; receiver-side text artifacts get unpredictable `os.CreateTemp`-style suffixes, so the practical target is a name the attacker knows (e.g. a file the user deliberately kept, or a name pattern from an earlier transfer the same peer sent). With the noisy prompt gone, the substitution is invisible to the user. Severity is bounded because the vulnerable names must start with the `croc-stdin-` prefix (dotfiles such as `.bashrc` cannot be named this way), so the attack cannot reach outside that namespace.

CVSS 3.1: `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:L` - base score 5.4 (Medium).
- **Attack Vector (AV): Network** - the sender is a remote peer; no local access needed.
- **Attack Complexity (AC): Low** - a crafted basename and a normal file transfer; no special conditions.
- **Privileges Required (PR): None** - the sender has no account on the receiver.
- **User Interaction (UI): Required** - the victim must run croc receive and accept the transfer.
- **Scope (S): Unchanged** - the vulnerable component is the croc receiver itself.
- **Confidentiality (C): None** - no read primitive; planted symlink targets are confined to the receive directory.
- **Integrity (I): Low** - the modification is limited to files whose names carry the `croc-stdin-` prefix, and it requires an exact-name collision with a pre-existing file; per CVSS 3.1, "can modify only certain files" is I:L - dotfiles such as `.bashrc` are unreachable.
- **Availability (A): Low** - the truncate-to-empty and remove-and-replace branches leave the previous file unavailable or destroyed. CWE-693 (Protection Mechanism Failure) is the root-cause classification: the overwrite protection mechanism is bypassed by a sender-controlled filename; CWE-73 (External Control of File Name or Path) is the companion classification and is the GHSA-selectable one (CWE-693 is not in GitHub's selectable set), while CWE-22 (path traversal) is not accurate here because writes stay confined to the receive root. Alternative reading: if the bounded namespace is scored as full integrity within reach - total content replacement of every colliding `croc-stdin-*` file - Integrity: High yields `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:L` = 7.1 (High).

## Reproduction Steps

Prerequisite: a Go toolchain satisfying `go.mod` (`go 1.27`) and a checkout of croc at commit `b6f27da9401f2c3647c1adb6b77a46bb8c0923d2`. The repro is a self-contained Go test that reuses the project's own in-process loopback test relay - the same harness as `TestCrocLocal` in `src/croc/croc_test.go` - so it requires no network, no third party, and no separately installed binary; it drives the exact production receive path (`NewCtx` + `Receive` -> receive-ready loop -> the gate at `src/croc/croc.go:3413`).

1. Save the following as `src/croc/repro_overwrite_bypass_test.go` in the checkout:

```go
package croc

import (
	"context"
	"fmt"
	"net"
	"os"
	"path/filepath"
	"testing"
	"time"

	log "github.com/schollz/croc/v11/src/logger"
)

// Repro: overwrite-confirmation bypass via a crafted "croc-stdin-" filename on receive.
func TestOverwriteConfirmationBypass(t *testing.T) {
	log.SetLevel("warn")
	localPorts := freeConsecutiveTestPorts(t, 2)
	localAddress := net.JoinHostPort("127.0.0.1", localPorts[0])

	victim := t.TempDir()
	attacker := t.TempDir()
	mustWrite := func(path, content string) {
		t.Helper()
		if err := os.WriteFile(path, []byte(content), 0o644); err != nil {
			t.Fatal(err)
		}
	}
	attackerStdin := filepath.Join(attacker, "croc-stdin-notes.txt")
	attackerCtrl := filepath.Join(attacker, "notes.txt")
	mustWrite(attackerStdin, "ATTACKER-REPLACEMENT\n")
	mustWrite(attackerCtrl, "ATTACKER-CONTROL\n")
	victimStdin := filepath.Join(victim, "croc-stdin-notes.txt")
	victimCtrl := filepath.Join(victim, "notes.txt")
	mustWrite(victimStdin, "ORIGINAL-CONTENT\n")
	mustWrite(victimCtrl, "ORIGINAL-CONTROL\n")

	// Receiver writes into its working directory (like `croc <code>` run in a folder).
	oldWD, err := os.Getwd()
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}
	if err := os.Chdir(victim); err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}
	defer func() { _ = os.Chdir(oldWD) }()

	sender, err := NewCtx(context.Background(), Options{
		IsSender:      true,
		SharedSecret:  "8123-testingthecroc",
		RelayAddress:  localAddress,
		RelayPorts:    append([]string(nil), localPorts...),
		RelayPassword: "pass123",
		NoPrompt:      true,
		DisableLocal:  false,
		OnlyLocal:     true,
		Curve:         "ed25519",
	})
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}
	// Default receive options: Overwrite=false, Rename=false. NoPrompt only
	// auto-accepts the transfer itself; it does NOT suppress the per-file
	// overwrite prompt (the code under test).
	receiver, err := NewCtx(context.Background(), Options{
		IsSender:      false,
		SharedSecret:  "8123-testingthecroc",
		RelayAddress:  localAddress,
		IP:            localAddress,
		RelayPassword: "pass123",
		NoPrompt:      true,
		DisableLocal:  false,
		Curve:         "ed25519",
	})
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}

	results := make(chan error, 2)
	go func() {
		filesInfo, emptyFolders, total, errGet := GetFilesInfo([]string{attackerStdin, attackerCtrl}, false, false, []string{})
		if errGet != nil {
			results <- errGet
			return
		}
		results <- sender.Send(filesInfo, emptyFolders, total)
	}()
	waitForRelayPorts(t, localPorts)
	go func() { results <- receiver.Receive() }()
	for i := 0; i < 2; i++ {
		select {
		case err := <-results:
			if err != nil {
				t.Fatalf("transfer %d failed: %v", i, err)
			}
		case <-time.After(60 * time.Second):
			t.Fatal("transfer timed out")
		}
	}
	time.Sleep(500 * time.Millisecond)

	gotStdin, _ := os.ReadFile(victimStdin)
	gotCtrl, _ := os.ReadFile(victimCtrl)
	fmt.Printf("OBSERVED croc-stdin-notes.txt: %q (no prompt)\n", string(gotStdin))
	fmt.Printf("OBSERVED notes.txt: %q (prompt fired; retained)\n", string(gotCtrl))

	if string(gotStdin) != "ATTACKER-REPLACEMENT\n" {
		t.Errorf("croc-stdin-notes.txt = %q, want %q (silent overwrite did not occur)", string(gotStdin), "ATTACKER-REPLACEMENT\n")
	}
	if string(gotCtrl) != "ORIGINAL-CONTROL\n" {
		t.Errorf("notes.txt = %q, want %q (prompt did not protect the control file)", string(gotCtrl), "ORIGINAL-CONTROL\n")
	}
}
```

2. Run it:

```bash
go test -count=1 -run TestOverwriteConfirmationBypass -v -timeout 150s ./src/croc/ </dev/null
```

3. Test output at pin `b6f27da9401f2c3647c1adb6b77a46bb8c0923d2` (2026-09-08):

```text
Resume 'notes.txt' (0.0%)? (y/N)   (use --overwrite to omit) Skipping 'notes.txt'
OBSERVED croc-stdin-notes.txt: "ATTACKER-REPLACEMENT\n" (no prompt)
OBSERVED notes.txt: "ORIGINAL-CONTROL\n" (prompt fired; retained)
--- PASS: TestOverwriteConfirmationBypass (1.04s)
PASS
```

What the differential shows: the transfer carries two ordinary files (not a text transfer - `SendingText` is false). One is named `croc-stdin-notes.txt` and collides with a pre-existing file in the receiver's directory; the other is named `notes.txt` and collides with another pre-existing file. For `notes.txt` the code printed the resume/overwrite confirmation (`Resume 'notes.txt' (0.0%)? (y/N) (use --overwrite to omit)`); with stdin closed (`</dev/null`, answer EOF) it skipped the file, which keeps its original content (`ORIGINAL-CONTROL`). For `croc-stdin-notes.txt` no prompt is printed at all, the loop falls through to `recipientInitializeFile` (src/croc/croc.go:3109), which opens the existing file `O_RDWR` (croc.go:3136-3138) and truncates/writes the sender's chunks - the file ends up holding exactly the attacker's content (`ATTACKER-REPLACEMENT`). The receiver here uses `NoPrompt=true` (the CLI `--yes` equivalent), which does not suppress this prompt: `askReceiveOverwrite` (src/croc/croc.go:3301) runs regardless of `NoPrompt`; only `--overwrite`, `--rename`, or the crafted `croc-stdin-` prefix suppress it.

Symlink / empty-file variant (v11.3.6 and later): with sender-declared metadata `fileInfo.Size == 0` or `fileInfo.Symlink != ""` for a file named `croc-stdin-<name>`, the skipped gate hands control to `createEmptyFileAndFinish` (src/croc/croc.go:3245), which removes any existing file at the destination (`root.Remove`, no prompt) and then creates an empty file or a symlink to the sender-supplied target. To exercise it, replace the attacker's regular file with an empty file or an in-directory symlink on the sender's side (e.g. `ln -s notes.txt src/croc-stdin-notes.txt`; note the target is validated by `validateReceiveSymlinkTarget`, croc.go:892, and must stay inside the receive directory) and re-run the same test; the regular-file case above already demonstrates the identical prompt-skip.

## Recommendations

Gate the exemption on the transfer actually being a text transfer, not on the received filename. In `src/croc/croc.go` the cleanest fix is to require both conditions before suppressing the prompt, e.g.:

```go
isStdinName := strings.HasPrefix(path.Base(fileInfo.Name), "croc-stdin-") && c.Options.SendingText
```

and make the empty-file/symlink branch (`createEmptyFileAndFinish`) and the `--rename` branch honor the same combined condition, so a regular file transfer can never claim the text-transfer exemption. As defense-in-depth, apply the same `SendingText` gate wherever a received `croc-stdin-*` name short-circuits a user confirmation, and document that the prefix is reserved for transfers the sender marked as text.

## Resources

- Source at pinned commit: https://github.com/schollz/croc/blob/b6f27da9401f2c3647c1adb6b77a46bb8c0923d2/src/croc/croc.go (prompt-gate ~L3405-3430; `createEmptyFileAndFinish` L3245-3280; `recipientInitializeFile` L3109-3160 (`os.O_RDWR` open at L3136-3138))
- Exemption origin: https://github.com/schollz/croc/commit/b687778d ("bug fix: doesn't ask overwrite text Fixes #384", 2021-04-29)
- `createEmptyFileAndFinish` origin (pre-gate, name-unrestricted until 615af377): https://github.com/schollz/croc/commit/6386e4a8
- Refactor that kept the exemption filename-only: https://github.com/schollz/croc/commit/615af377 ("fix: gate overwrites and receive hash algorithms", 2026-08-29, first released v11.3.6)
- Prior related disclosure (arbitrary file deletion via `croc-marked-files.txt`, fixed 11.0.3 by c0d51f0, different sink and mechanism): oss-sec 2026/Q3 #497 - https://seclists.org/oss-sec/2026/q3/497
- Related prior advisory in the same class (sender-controlled names reaching the filesystem, fixed 9.6.16, does not cover this prompt bypass): GHSA-ppjh-xp5v-46wc (CVE-2023-43619)

items.title: Moleculer: Unauthenticated Denial of Service via negative length field in the TCP transporter packet parser
items.description:
### Summary

The TCP transporter's packet parser (`src/transporters/tcp/parser.js`) reads the packet length field with `Buffer.prototype.readInt32BE`, a signed read. A crafted packet whose length field has the sign bit set yields a negative `length`. The parser then advances past the parsed message with `packet = packet.slice(length)`, but `Buffer.prototype.slice` clamps an out-of-range negative start index to `0`, so the buffer is returned unchanged. The `while (packet.length > 0)` loop condition therefore never becomes false, producing an infinite synchronous loop that blocks the Node.js event loop indefinitely.

### Impact

Any Moleculer node using the TCP transporter can be rendered completely unresponsive by an unauthenticated remote peer sending a single ~10-byte crafted TCP packet, before any protocol handshake or authentication takes place. `TcpReader.onTcpClientConnected` pipes each accepted socket's bytes straight into a fresh `Parser` instance (`socket.pipe(parser)`) with no handshake, so the code path is reachable by any peer able to reach the transporter's listening port. Because Node.js is single-threaded, the hang blocks the entire event loop of the process, taking down every service hosted in it until it is forcibly restarted. TCP transporter endpoints are frequently auto-discovered via UDP broadcast, so any host on the same network segment can reach the port.

Neither the CRC check nor `maxPacketSize` mitigate the issue: the CRC bytes are fully attacker-computable, and `maxPacketSize` bounds the received buffer size, not the value of the length field.

### Affected component

`Parser._write` in `src/transporters/tcp/parser.js`.

### Patch

The fix validates that the decoded length is at least the 6-byte header size before processing, rejecting negative and undersized values (which would otherwise fail to shrink the buffer) with an error on the write callback instead of looping.

### Credit

Reported by xor4xor via the Tidelift security program.

items.title: The NXP ENET-QOS Ethernet driver's receive work handler eth_nxp_enet_qos_rx() in drivers/ethernet/eth_nxp_enet_qos hand…
items.description:
The NXP ENET-QOS Ethernet driver's receive work handler eth_nxp_enet_qos_rx() in drivers/ethernet/eth_nxp_enet_qos hands each processed descriptor back to the DMA by writing desc->read.control = rx_desc_refresh_flags, which sets OWN_FLAG and BUF1_ADDR_VALID_FLAG. RDES0 of a receive descriptor is the DMA buffer address in read format, but the hardware write-back aliases that word with the VLAN tag fields (or, for a context descriptor, the timestamp low word), so it is destroyed on every completion. The success path rewrites desc->read.buf1_addr before re-arming; the four drop paths — errored or non-first descriptor, net_pkt_rx_alloc() failure, invalid descriptor length, and net_pkt_get_frag() failure — did not, re-arming the ring slot with the write-back residue as its DMA target address.

The drop paths are driven entirely by received traffic and need no privilege or special configuration. With the defaults for this driver (CONFIG_NET_BUF_DATA_SIZE of 128 and 16 receive descriptors) a single full-size frame consumes twelve ring slots and twelve K_NO_WAIT fragment allocations, so a short burst of frames sent to the device exhausts the receive pools and reaches the allocation-failure paths; a frame with a receive error, or any frame whose first descriptor was already dropped, reaches the non-first-descriptor path.

Once a slot has been poisoned, the DMA writes the next frame received in that slot to an address derived from the frame's VLAN tag fields rather than to a receive buffer. On the supported MCX SoCs that address falls in flash or reserved space, so the transfer raises a fatal bus error that the driver only logs — there is no reset or recovery path — and reception stops permanently until the device is rebooted; where the write is silently discarded instead, the untouched buffer is later handed to the network stack with a length, delivering stale buffer contents as if they were a received frame. A single triggering event is enough to make the condition persistent, so an attacker able to send traffic to the device can permanently disable its network interface.

items.title: The NXP ENET QoS Ethernet driver in drivers/ethernet/eth_nxp_enet_qos serialises transmission with a binary semaphore,…
items.description:
The NXP ENET QoS Ethernet driver in drivers/ethernet/eth_nxp_enet_qos serialises transmission with a binary semaphore, data->tx.tx_sem, taken in eth_nxp_enet_qos_tx() and returned only by the transmit-completion interrupt handler tx_dma_done(). A frame that has been handed to the transmit DMA when the Ethernet link goes down is never written back, so that completion interrupt never arrives. The PHY callback eth_nxp_enet_qos_phy_cb() reacts to carrier loss only by calling net_eth_carrier_set(); it does not stop the DMA, take the descriptors back or release the outstanding frame, and no timeout exists to do so.

The trigger is a link-down/link-up transition that lands while a frame is under the transmit DMA. It can be produced by anyone who controls the link partner or the cable — for example by administratively downing and restoring the attached switch port, or by restarting auto-negotiation from a peer device — and can be made reliable by generating traffic that keeps the device transmitting and repeating the transition. No credentials or user interaction are required, and the trigger is at the link layer rather than over IP.

Because the semaphore is never given back, every subsequent call to eth_nxp_enet_qos_tx() fails with -EBUSY for the remaining life of the boot; restoring the link does not recover the interface, since the link-up path only rewrites MAC_CONFIGURATION. The affected interface continues to receive but can no longer transmit anything — no ARP replies, no TCP acknowledgements, no DHCP renewals — until the device is reset. The net_pkt and the net_buf fragments of the abandoned frame are likewise never unreferenced and never return to their pools. The security-relevant property is persistence: a momentary link flap leaves the interface permanently unable to send, so the denial of service outlasts the attacker's access to the link. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact.

The fix adds a claim/release pair around the outstanding packet so that completion and abandonment are mutually exclusive, aborts an outstanding frame from the PHY callback on carrier loss (stopping the DMA, flushing the MTL transmit queue and reinitialising the descriptor ring), and arms a transmit watchdog, CONFIG_ETH_NXP_ENET_QOS_TX_TIMEOUT_MS, so that any non-completing DMA — not only a carrier loss — reclaims the transmit slot and the packet.

items.title: When CONFIG_THREAD_STACK_MEM_MAPPED is enabled, each thread stack is mapped into the kernel virtual address space with…
items.description:
When CONFIG_THREAD_STACK_MEM_MAPPED is enabled, each thread stack is mapped into the kernel virtual address space with a guard page on either side, and the mapping is released during abort cleanup. k_thread_abort_cleanup() in kernel/thread.c has two paths: a deferred one for self-abort, which stashes the mapping in thread_cleanup_stack_addr/thread_cleanup_stack_sz, and an immediate one for a thread aborted by some other thread. The immediate path called do_thread_cleanup(), which ignored its thread argument and only ever unmapped the stashed address — a value populated exclusively by the self-abort path. The mapped stack of a thread aborted by another thread was therefore never unmapped.

Every k_thread_abort() of a non-current thread leaks the thread's stack region plus its two guard pages from the kernel virtual address space. Threads that end by returning from their entry function take the working self-abort path, so the leak is specific to explicit cancellation — k_thread_abort(), pthread_cancel(), osThreadTerminate(), or the kernel thread kill shell command. Both k_thread_create() and k_thread_abort() are system calls, so with CONFIG_USERSPACE an unprivileged user-mode thread that has been granted a thread object and a user-capable stack object can drive the leak from user mode, consuming a kernel-side resource it cannot otherwise touch.

With CONFIG_KERNEL_VM_SIZE defaulting to 8 MB, a few hundred create/abort cycles exhaust the runtime mapping region. k_mem_map_phys_guard() then returns NULL, and map_thread_stack() guards that only with __ASSERT_NO_MSG(), which is compiled out of production builds; thread creation proceeds to write through a NULL-derived stack base and faults in kernel mode. The impact is a persistent denial of service — a kernel fatal error requiring a reboot — with no memory disclosure or corruption, and it is limited to configurations where memory-mapped thread stacks are enabled (x86 targets with X86_MMU and demand paging disabled, where the option is implied by default).

items.title: The HTTP client's debug helper print_header_field() in subsys/net/lib/http/http_client.c formatted an http_parser data-…
items.description:
The HTTP client's debug helper print_header_field() in subsys/net/lib/http/http_client.c formatted an http_parser data-callback slice with a %s conversion: snprintk(output, len + 1, "%s", str). The parser hands its callbacks a pointer and a length into the caller's receive buffer, and those bytes are not NUL terminated. The size argument of snprintk() bounds only the destination, while the %s conversion measures the source first — lib/os/cbprintf_complete.c uses strlen() when no precision is given, and lib/os/cbprintf_nano.c uses strlen() unconditionally — so the read walks past the end of the header field and past the end of the receive buffer until it finds a zero byte.

The slice reaches the helper from on_url(), on_header_field() and on_header_value(), which the parser invokes on bytes that http_wait_data() read straight off the socket into the application-supplied recv_buf. A malicious or compromised HTTP server, or an attacker able to answer a plaintext request, therefore controls both the header field and the bytes that follow it in the buffer, and can guarantee that no zero byte appears before the buffer ends, forcing the over-read. The in-tree tests/net/lib/http_client suite reproduces the over-read under CONFIG_ASAN=y on an ordinary GET.

The impact is bounded. The whole helper body is compiled only when the HTTP client log module is explicitly set to Debug (CONFIG_NET_HTTP_LOG_LEVEL_DBG=y, which the global CONFIG_LOG_DEFAULT_LEVEL does not set), so default builds are unaffected. No out-of-bounds write occurs and none of the over-read bytes are emitted into the log, so there is no information disclosure; the consequence is an out-of-bounds read that can fault and panic the device where the buffer abuts an unmapped or MPU/MMU-protected region.

The fix copies exactly the len bytes the parser offered with memcpy() and terminates them, instead of relying on a %s conversion (a %.*s precision would not have sufficed, since cbprintf_nano.c measures the source in full before applying it).

items.title: The Xtensa MMU userspace port never initialized the per-thread page-table pointer thread->arch.ptables during thread se…
items.description:
The Xtensa MMU userspace port never initialized the per-thread page-table pointer thread->arch.ptables during thread setup, while arch_mem_domain_thread_add() in arch/xtensa/core/ptables.c uses a non-NULL value of that field as its "this thread is migrating from another memory domain" predicate. For a thread whose struct k_thread backing memory is not zeroed, the field holds stale data and the kernel takes the migration branch, passing that stale value to reset_region() as the base of a level-1 page table. The equivalent field on x86 is explicitly cleared in z_x86_userspace_prepare_thread() for exactly this reason; the Xtensa port adopted the predicate without the initialization.

The condition is reachable from an unprivileged user-mode thread on a build with CONFIG_XTENSA_MMU, CONFIG_USERSPACE and dynamically allocated kernel objects. k_object_alloc(K_OBJ_THREAD) is a system call and allocates the thread object from the caller's resource pool without zeroing it, and the k_thread_create() verifier accepts such an object while forcing the K_USER option, so the migration branch is taken whenever the recycled heap bytes at that offset are non-zero. Because a user thread can also allocate, fill and free other kernel objects from the same heap, the stale bytes are groomable rather than merely random.

Walking the bogus table in region_map_update() performs an unguarded index into l2_page_tables_counter[], may copy from and write through the attacker-influenceable level-1 base in dup_l2_table_if_needed(), and finally writes a page-table entry through a second pointer read out of that memory — once per page of the new thread's stack. The result is out-of-bounds reads and writes executed in supervisor mode, ranging from an immediate kernel panic (observed as Xtensa EXCAUSE 13 on Intel ADSP DSP firmware with user threads) to corruption of kernel memory and escape from the user-mode sandbox.

items.title: The Renesas RA SCI UART driver's receive-error ISR, uart_ra_sci_eri_isr() in drivers/serial/uart_renesas_ra_sci.c, ackn…
items.description:
The Renesas RA SCI UART driver's receive-error ISR, uart_ra_sci_eri_isr() in drivers/serial/uart_renesas_ra_sci.c, acknowledged the error condition only when a Zephyr interrupt-driven callback had already been registered. With CONFIG_UART_INTERRUPT_DRIVEN=y and CONFIG_UART_ASYNC_API=n, if data->user_cb is NULL the ISR body is empty: the SCI error flags (SSR.ORER, SSR.FER, SSR.PER) are left set and the ICU event flag R_ICU->IELSR_b[eri_irq].IR is never cleared, so the interrupt re-pends immediately and the ISR is re-entered without end.

The error interrupt is masked at boot by uart_ra_sci_init(), but FSP's R_SCI_UART_Open() unconditionally re-enables it, and uart_ra_sci_configure() - the back end of the public uart_configure() API, enabled by default via CONFIG_UART_USE_RUNTIME_CONFIGURE - performs a Close()/Open() pair without re-masking it. Any runtime uart_configure() therefore leaves the error interrupt live regardless of whether a callback has been set, as does calling uart_irq_err_enable() on its own. An instance used with the polling API, or the window between uart_configure() and uart_irq_callback_user_data_set(), thus runs with the error interrupt unmasked and no callback registered.

The trigger is an ordinary receive line error - overrun, framing, parity, or a break condition - which is fully determined by the device attached to the serial link. A peer able to assert a break or transmit at a mismatched baud rate produces such an error at will, so a single frame is enough to enter the state.

The impact is availability only: the CPU is captured in the re-entering ISR and never returns to thread context, hanging the entire system until an external reset or hardware watchdog fires. There is no memory corruption or information disclosure. Builds using the asynchronous UART API are unaffected, because the fall-through to FSP's sci_uart_eri_isr() clears both the error flags and the pending IRQ.

items.title: usbh_device_init() in subsys/usb/host/usbh_device.c rejects a device whose device descriptor advertises bNumConfigurati…
items.description:
usbh_device_init() in subsys/usb/host/usbh_device.c rejects a device whose device descriptor advertises bNumConfigurations == 0, but it only logs the error and jumps to the cleanup label without setting the return code. At that point the local err is still 0 from the preceding successful descriptor read, so the function returns success while having skipped usbh_device_set_configuration() — the only place udev->cfg_desc is allocated. The device structure is zero-initialised by usbh_device_alloc(), so udev->cfg_desc remains NULL.

usbh_device_connect() treats the zero return as a successful enumeration and calls usbh_class_probe_device(), which starts its descriptor walk from udev->cfg_desc. usbh_desc_get_next_function() passes that NULL pointer to usbh_desc_is_valid(), whose only guard compares the caller-supplied size, so head->bLength is read through a NULL pointer.

The condition is triggered entirely by the attached peripheral: attaching a USB device (or any USB gadget emulating one) that reports bNumConfigurations = 0 reaches the defect directly from the UHC_EVT_DEV_CONNECTED_FS/_HS event handler in subsys/usb/host/usbh_core.c, with no authentication and no user interaction beyond the physical attachment.

On targets where page zero is unmapped or CONFIG_NULL_POINTER_EXCEPTION_DETECTION is enabled this raises a fatal exception in the USB host thread, denying service to the host. Where address zero is readable, the descriptor walker instead parses low memory as a descriptor chain and can dispatch a class probe() with attacker-influenced values, causing further out-of-bounds reads through the still-NULL udev->cfg_desc in usbh_desc_get_iface(). No attacker-controlled write was identified, so the impact is availability plus a bounded out-of-bounds read. Note that CONFIG_USB_HOST_STACK is marked experimental.

items.title: In apport before 2.37.0, an improper privilege management vulnerability allows an unprivileged local attacker to gain r…
items.description: In apport before 2.37.0, an improper privilege management vulnerability allows an unprivileged local attacker to gain root privileges on systems where automatic crash reporting is enabled. The automatic crash report processing pipeline runs as root and executes ldd on the attacker-controlled ExecutablePath field of a crash file placed in the world-writable /var/crash directory, causing the dynamic loader to load and execute an attacker-supplied audit module specified by the ELF's DT_AUDIT tag. This allows an attacker to execute arbitrary code with root privileges and fully compromise the affected system.

items.title: In apport before 2.37.0, a path traversal vulnerability allows an attacker who can supply a crafted crash report to cau…
items.description:
In apport before 2.37.0, a path traversal vulnerability allows an attacker who can supply a crafted crash report to cause unintended file creation or overwrite outside the intended extraction directory when the report is processed with apport-unpack.

The key-name validation added for CVE-2026-77113 does not cover base64-encoded keys skipped by ProblemReport.load(binary=False), and ProblemReport.extract_keys() writes them to a file path built from the key without validation. This allows an attacker to create or overwrite arbitrary files writable by the invoking user, such as .bashrc or .profile, gaining persistence or code execution in that user's context.

items.title: ModSecurity is an open source, cross platform web application firewall (WAF) engine for Apache, IIS and Nginx.
items.description: ModSecurity is an open source, cross platform web application firewall (WAF) engine for Apache, IIS and Nginx. From 3.0.15 until 3.0.17, XML request body processing with SecParseXmlIntoArgs set to On or OnlyArgs can leave XMLNodes::parsing_ctx_arg uninitialized in the SAX end-element callback. A single crafted unauthenticated HTTP request can make a worker dereference the pointer, resulting in a constant-value write to an attacker-controlled address. The resulting memory corruption can terminate the worker and may disclose memory or redirect execution. Earlier 3.0.x releases and ModSecurity 2.x do not use the affected path. This issue is fixed in version 3.0.17.

items.title: AsyncSSH is a Python package which provides an asynchronous client and server implementation of the SSHv2 protocol on t…
items.description: AsyncSSH is a Python package which provides an asynchronous client and server implementation of the SSHv2 protocol on top of the Python asyncio framework. Prior to 2.24.1, recursive remote-to-local SFTP copies in SFTPClient._copy() in asyncssh/sftp.py, reached through get(), mget(), and copy(), trust filenames returned by a remote server's directory enumeration. A malicious or compromised SFTP server can return an absolute filename or a filename containing path separators and parent-directory traversal, causing destination path construction to escape the requested local directory and write attacker-selected content to locations writable by the client process. This issue is fixed in version 2.24.1.

items.title: augment-virShell allows Command Injection in `grep()` via Unsanitized `searchPattern`
items.description: augment-vir is a collection of helper functions. Prior to version 31.73.5, the grep() function exported by @augment-vir/node inserts caller-controlled search patterns directly into a double-quoted shell command string without sanitization (grep.ts:310). When the constructed command is passed to spawn() with shell: 'bash' (shell.ts:98-99), bash evaluates $() command substitution expressions embedded in the pattern, resulting in arbitrary OS command execution as the Node.js process user. Any downstream application that passes untrusted input to grep()'s pattern or patterns field is vulnerable to unauthenticated local (and potentially remote) code execution. This issue has been patched in version 31.73.5.

items.title: bird-lg-go is a BIRD looking glass in Go.
items.description: bird-lg-go is a BIRD looking glass in Go. Prior to version 1.4.7, unsanitized input path enables arbitrary local file read, allowing an unauthenticated remote attacker to read sensitive files such as /etc/shadow and /root/.bash_history. This issue has been patched in version 1.4.7.

items.title: pympp allows excessive sponsored transaction fees through padded calldata
items.description: pympp is a Python SDK for the Machine Payments Protocol. Prior to version 0.9.1, when the server acts as the fee_payer, pympp validates calldata using eth_abi decoding, which is lenient about trailing bytes. The FeePayerPolicy caps gas_limit (≤ 2 M) and max_fee_per_gas (≤ 100 Gwei) but does not check calldata length. Tempo uses legacy calldata gas pricing: 16 gas per non-zero byte. Appending N bytes of 0x01 padding inflates actual gas used by N × 16 while keeping gas_limit and max_fee_per_gas within policy caps. The server cosigns and broadcasts the padded transaction, draining its fee-payer wallet. This issue has been patched in version 0.9.1.

items.title: ModSecurity is an open source, cross platform web application firewall (WAF) engine for Apache, IIS and Nginx.
items.description: ModSecurity is an open source, cross platform web application firewall (WAF) engine for Apache, IIS and Nginx. Prior to 2.9.15 and 3.0.17, t:htmlEntityDecode recognizes only a small subset of named HTML entities, so rules that depend on the transformation can inspect different bytes than a browser or backend. Attackers can encode ASCII separators and operators with unhandled entity names, including aliases, to bypass rules that depend on the transformation. The v3 decoder also accepts prefix matches instead of requiring an exact entity-token length, which can transform invalid longer names into different bytes. This issue is fixed in versions 2.9.15 and 3.0.17.

items.title: titra is an open source time tracking project.
items.description: titra is an open source time tracking project. In versions 1.0.3 and prior, authenticated API users can abuse the customfields object to inject or overwrite top-level fields in MongoDB documents. At time of publication, there are no publicly known patches.

items.title: Replicate Cog through 0.23.1 contains a server-side request forgery vulnerability that allows attackers to cause the Co…
items.description: Replicate Cog through 0.23.1 contains a server-side request forgery vulnerability that allows attackers to cause the Cog process to make server-side HTTP requests by submitting prediction inputs with attacker-controlled URLs that are not validated against the resolved destination host or IP before fetching. Attackers can supply malicious URLs or exploit HTTP redirects in cog.File and cog.Path predictor inputs to force requests to internal addresses, potentially exposing sensitive internal services or credentials.

items.title: Rack: Multipart parsing allows DoS via unbounded scan buffer growth
items.description: Rack is a modular Ruby web server interface. Prior to 2.2.25, 3.1.23, and 3.2.8, Rack::Multipart::Parser can retain parsed data in its internal StringScanner buffer when reads end inside or immediately after multipart headers. An unauthenticated attacker can align many small parts with rack.multipart.buffer_size boundaries so the buffer grows with the request despite per-field, header, and preamble limits, causing a worker to exhaust memory. The attack requires only a well-formed multipart body and affects applications that parse multipart requests. This issue is fixed in versions 2.2.25, 3.1.23, and 3.2.8.

items.title: Rack: Rack::Static header_rules bypass via dot-segment normalization mismatch
items.description: Rack is a modular Ruby web server interface. Prior to 2.2.25, 3.1.23, and 3.2.8, Rack::Static serves a path after Utils.clean_path_info normalization but evaluates header_rules against a path that is only URL-decoded. An unauthenticated attacker can request a known file through raw or percent-encoded dot segments and receive it without path-specific security headers such as Content-Disposition or Content-Security-Policy. Applications that do not use path-specific header_rules are not affected. This issue is fixed in versions 2.2.25, 3.1.23, and 3.2.8.

items.title: Rack: Rack::Request#host_with_port (and #base_url / #url) return the raw invalid Host header — incomplete fix of CVE-2026-34835
items.description: Rack is a modular Ruby web server interface. From 3.0 until 3.1.23 and 3.2.8, Rack::Request#host_with_port, #base_url, and #url can return an attacker-controlled invalid authority from Host, X-Forwarded-Host, or Forwarded: host= verbatim. Applications without an independent host allowlist that use these methods for absolute URLs, redirects, or origin-dependent checks can emit attacker-chosen delimiters, enabling redirect manipulation, string-based allowlist bypass, or unescaped markup reflection. Rails overrides these methods and is not expected to be affected. This issue is fixed in versions 3.1.23 and 3.2.8.

items.title: djust provides Phoenix LiveView-style reactive server-side rendering for Django with Rust-powered performance.
items.description: djust provides Phoenix LiveView-style reactive server-side rendering for Django with Rust-powered performance. Prior to versions 1.0.10 and 1.1.2, djust keys context output-safety grants by variable name and fails to revoke a grant when a template bind replaces the value associated with that name. A template using {% with %}, {% for %}, {% include ... with %}, tuple unpacking, or assign tags can therefore rebind a name that previously held mark_safe content and emit the new attacker-controlled value without escaping, including descendant lookups through the rebound name. This can cause stored or reflected cross-site scripting when a victim renders the affected template. This issue is fixed in versions 1.0.10 and 1.1.2.

items.title: Muhammara is a node module with c/cpp bindings to modify PDF with JavaScript for node or electron.
items.description: Muhammara is a node module with c/cpp bindings to modify PDF with JavaScript for node or electron. Prior to 6.0.5, Muhammara PDFParser::CreateFilterForStream() in src/deps/PDFWriter/PDFParser.cpp dereferences a null PDFInteger pointer when a PDF stream uses the LZWDecode filter with a DecodeParms dictionary that omits the EarlyChange key. An application that processes an untrusted PDF and reads the affected stream can crash, causing a denial of service. This issue is fixed in version 6.0.5.

items.title: Wagtail is an open source content management system built on Django.
items.description: Wagtail is an open source content management system built on Django. Prior to 7.0.9, 7.3.4, 7.4.3, and 8.0rc2, a Wagtail CMS user with the submit translations permission can call the Admin API copy for translation action for a source page that the user cannot edit. The action copies the inaccessible page into a translation, allowing the user to view its contents despite the missing source-page edit permission. This issue is fixed in versions 7.0.9, 7.3.4, 7.4.3, and 8.0rc2.

items.title: Wagtail is an open source content management system built on Django.
items.description: Wagtail is an open source content management system built on Django. Prior to 7.0.9, 7.3.4, 7.4.3, and 8.0rc2, Wagtail applies ETag conditional request processing to the document serve endpoint before document permission and filename checks complete. An unauthenticated attacker who knows a document ID and a candidate SHA1 hash can submit If-Match or If-None-Match and distinguish the response, revealing whether that hash is present in the document library. The issue does not expose document contents, filenames, other metadata, or information about hashes the attacker does not already know. This issue is fixed in versions 7.0.9, 7.3.4, 7.4.3, and 8.0rc2.

items.title: Rack: Multipart boundary ambiguity guard in Rack::Multipart::Parser can be bypassed with a quoted boundary value, allowing WAF bypass
items.description: Rack is a modular Ruby web server interface. Prior to 2.2.25, 3.1.23, and 3.2.8, Rack::Multipart::Parser.parse_boundary can skip a leading empty or quoted boundary parameter in a multipart Content-Type header and accept a later parameter. Rack can therefore parse a request body with a boundary that a conforming intermediary would not derive, allowing form fields or file uploads to reach an application without the intended proxy or web application firewall inspection. This issue is fixed in versions 2.2.25, 3.1.23, and 3.2.8.

items.title: A weakness has been identified in Turboderp-org ExLlamaV3 up to 1.6.3.
items.description: A weakness has been identified in Turboderp-org ExLlamaV3 up to 1.6.3. The impacted element is the function routing_sel_norm_kernel of the file exllamav3/exllamav3_ext/routing.cu of the component hash-MoE routing. This manipulation of the argument gate.tid2eid causes out-of-bounds read. Remote exploitation of the attack is possible. Upgrading to version 1.6.4 is sufficient to resolve this issue. Patch name: c9a57ae832a3035e264e0a412e1daf4ebb699b98. Upgrading the affected component is recommended.

items.title: A security flaw has been discovered in Turboderp-org ExLlamaV3 up to 1.6.3.
items.description: A security flaw has been discovered in Turboderp-org ExLlamaV3 up to 1.6.3. The affected element is the function ngram_dequant of the file exllamav3/exllamav3_ext/ngram.cu of the component NGramEmbedding. The manipulation of the argument head_bias results in out-of-bounds read. The attack may be launched remotely. The exploit has been released to the public and may be used for attacks. Upgrading to version 1.6.4 is sufficient to fix this issue. The patch is identified as c9a57ae832a3035e264e0a412e1daf4ebb699b98. It is suggested to upgrade the affected component.

items.title: A security vulnerability has been detected in braindecode up to 1.8.2.
items.description: A security vulnerability has been detected in braindecode up to 1.8.2. This affects the function EEGModuleMixin._from_pretrained of the file braindecode/models/base.py of the component Hub Integration. Such manipulation of the argument filename leads to path traversal. The attack can be executed remotely. The exploit has been disclosed publicly and may be used. Upgrading to version 2.0.0 mitigates this issue. The name of the patch is 05b764d93b9a50400f523206fbe03d73d0cf5edb. It is recommended to upgrade the affected component.

items.title: A vulnerability was identified in nushell up to 0.116.1.
items.description: A vulnerability was identified in nushell up to 0.116.1. Impacted is the function escape_bytes of the file crates/nu-json/src/ser.rs of the component Data Conversion Handler. The manipulation leads to improper neutralization of escape, meta, or control sequences. The attack must be carried out locally. The pull request to fix this issue awaits acceptance.

items.title: Aiohttp Aiohttp: AIOHTTP is an asynchronous HTTP client/server framework for asyncio and Python.
items.description: AIOHTTP is an asynchronous HTTP client/server framework for asyncio and Python. Prior to 3.14.4, the WebSocket reader retains one bytes object for each transport read while reassembling an incomplete frame. A malicious peer can split a frame into many tiny reads so per-object overhead substantially exceeds the payload bytes allowed by max_msg_size. The condition affects a server receiving frames from a malicious client and a client receiving frames from a malicious server, and can cause excessive memory consumption or denial of service. This issue is fixed in version 3.14.4.

items.title: pyLoad is a free and open-source download manager written in Python.
items.description: pyLoad is a free and open-source download manager written in Python. Prior to 0.5.0b3.dev101, Api.check_apikey caches successful validation in self._apikey_cache using only the attacker-controlled key_id. After a legitimate key populates the cache, a forged API key with the same key_id reaches the cache-hit path without comparing apikey[-43:] to the stored hash through hmac.compare_digest. Key identifiers are small sequential integers, so an unauthenticated remote attacker can enumerate an active identifier and inherit the cached key owner's permissions during the 300-second cache lifetime. This issue is fixed in version 0.5.0b3.dev101.

items.title: LMDeploy is a toolkit for compressing, deploying, and serving large language models.
items.description: LMDeploy is a toolkit for compressing, deploying, and serving large language models. From 0.12.3 until 0.15.0, _is_safe_url validates remote media URLs with urlparse while requests.Session().get interprets backslashes differently when sending the request. An attacker can provide a URL whose validation hostname appears globally routable but whose request destination resolves to an internal host, bypassing non-global address checks. Applications that accept attacker-controlled remote media URLs can therefore be induced to access internal HTTP services and expose data available from those services. This issue is fixed in version 0.15.0.

items.title: Wagtail is an open source content management system built on Django.
items.description: Wagtail is an open source content management system built on Django. Prior to 7.0.9, 7.3.4, 7.4.3, and 8.0rc2, a CMS user who has add permission for a snippet model but lacks change and view permission for an existing snippet can access the snippet copy view and copy that source object. The copy operation reveals the contents of a snippet that the user is not authorized to view. This issue is fixed in versions 7.0.9, 7.3.4, 7.4.3, and 8.0rc2.

items.title: The export-cluster-logs and export-image-logs commands in the AWS ParallelCluster CLI before version 3.16.0 contain a r…
items.description:
The export-cluster-logs and export-image-logs commands in the AWS ParallelCluster CLI before version 3.16.0 contain a relative path traversal issue. An authenticated remote user with write access to the log export Amazon S3 bucket could use a crafted S3 object key to write files outside the intended export directory on the machine running the command. The written files would have names and content controlled by a third party, and would be created with the privileges of the user running the command.



To remediate this issue, users should upgrade to version 3.16.0 or later.

items.title: Wagtail is an open source content management system built on Django.
items.description: Wagtail is an open source content management system built on Django. Prior to 7.0.9, 7.3.4, 7.4.3, and 8.0rc2, the Wagtail Documents and Images API V2 excludes directly restricted collections but fails to exclude their descendant collections, even though descendants inherit ancestor view restrictions. An API user can therefore list the filenames and names of documents and images stored in descendant collections that should remain private. This issue is fixed in versions 7.0.9, 7.3.4, 7.4.3, and 8.0rc2.

items.title: pyLoad is a free and open-source download manager written in Python.
items.description: pyLoad is a free and open-source download manager written in Python. Prior to 0.5.0b3.dev102, UnTar._safe_extractall in src/pyload/plugins/extractors/UnTar.py validates archive member paths and link targets but does not call TarInfo.isdev to reject special tar member types before calling tarfile.extractall. On supported Python 3.9 through 3.13 runtimes, tarfile defaults to the fully_trusted extraction filter, so a user with ADD and STATUS permissions can cause extraction of a crafted archive containing character devices, block devices, or FIFOs. Python 3.14 defaults to a safe extraction filter. When pyLoad runs with operating-system privileges that permit device creation, including the official root-based Docker deployment, the archive can expose raw devices and compromise the host. Non-root deployments can still create FIFOs that cause hangs or IPC confusion. This issue is fixed in version 0.5.0b3.dev102.

items.title: Dynatrace MCP Server is an MCP server for Dynatrace Observability.
items.description: Dynatrace MCP Server is an MCP server for Dynatrace Observability. Prior to 2.0.0, a server started with the --http option accepts JSON-RPC tools/call requests without authentication, session validation, or Host and Origin protections before dispatching them under the server's configured Dynatrace credentials. A network-reachable caller can invoke execute_dql to read logs, security events, user sessions, and other Grail data, or invoke create_dynatrace_notebook to create tenant-visible notebooks. The send_event path is not affected because its requestHumanApproval gate blocks this attack path, and reset_grail_budget only demonstrates dispatch without accessing Dynatrace data. This issue is fixed in version 2.0.0.

items.title: pyLoad is a free and open-source download manager written in Python.
items.description: pyLoad is a free and open-source download manager written in Python. Prior to 0.5.0b3.dev102, pyLoad does not invalidate existing Flask sessions when an administrator changes a user's permissions or password through /api/set_user_permission or /api/change_password. Api.set_user_permission and Api.change_password update the database, but session authorization continues to use role and permission values copied at login by set_session in webui/app/helpers.py. A user can therefore retain revoked privileges or continue using a session established with an old password for the configured session lifetime. API-key authentication is not affected because that path rereads user data from the database. This issue is fixed in version 0.5.0b3.dev102.

items.title: pyLoad is a free and open-source download manager written in Python.
items.description: pyLoad is a free and open-source download manager written in Python. Prior to 0.5.0b3.dev102, an authenticated non-admin user with the SETTINGS permission can configure WindowsPhoneNotify through /json/save_config by setting pushurl, pushid, and enabled. WindowsPhoneNotify.send in src/pyload/plugins/addons/WindowsPhoneNotify.py then uses http.client.HTTPConnection without pyLoad's pycurl destination validation. When a download completes, the global notification event causes a blind POST from the pyLoad server to the attacker-selected internal host, port, and path. The response is not returned, but the request can probe internal services, reach cloud metadata endpoints, or trigger state-changing internal HTTP endpoints. This issue is fixed in version 0.5.0b3.dev102.

items.title: Dynatrace MCP Server is an MCP server for Dynatrace Observability.
items.description: Dynatrace MCP Server is an MCP server for Dynatrace Observability. Prior to 2.1.1, several read capabilities interpolate caller-controlled values into DQL without sufficient validation or escaping. The src/capabilities/find-monitored-entity-by-name.ts capability embeds entityNames in string searches, src/capabilities/list-problems.ts, src/capabilities/list-vulnerabilities.ts, and src/capabilities/list-exceptions.ts embed timeframe values, and src/capabilities/get-events-for-cluster.ts embeds timeframe, clusterId, and kubernetesEntityId. Crafted values can close string literals, append pipeline stages, or comment out the remaining intended query, allowing callers to bypass field selection, time-window, and result-display limits in tools marked readOnlyHint. The issue does not grant data access beyond the configured token's existing execute_dql capability, but it breaks the narrower auto-approved tool contract. This issue is fixed in version 2.1.1.

items.title: Dynatrace MCP Server is an MCP server for Dynatrace Observability.
items.description: Dynatrace MCP Server is an MCP server for Dynatrace Observability. Prior to 1.8.7, the create_dynatrace_notebook registration in src/index.ts performs a persistent document-write action without calling requestHumanApproval, although the project's other write tools use that gate to obtain operator consent. A caller can create tenant-visible notebooks containing attacker-controlled Markdown or DQL content, and tenant users may later execute embedded DQL when opening the notebook. The tool also lacks a destructiveHint annotation that would signal its side effects to MCP clients. This issue is fixed in version 1.8.7.

items.title: Signal K Server is a server application that runs on a central hub in a boat.
items.description: Signal K Server is a server application that runs on a central hub in a boat. From 2.0.0 until 2.34.0 for Signal K Server and from 1.0.0 until 1.5.3 for @signalk/resources-provider, the v2 REST route GET /signalk/v2/api/resources/:resourceType/:resourceId accepts an unsafe resourceId that can escape the intended resource directory. The route passes the attacker-controlled resourceId through src/api/resources/index.ts to FileStore.getResource() in packages/resources-provider-plugin/src/filestorage.ts without adequate path containment, allowing arbitrary JSON files reachable by the server to be read. Related PUT and DELETE resource operations can write or delete files outside the storage root. Deployments with allow_readonly enabled permit anonymous reads, while other deployments require a readonly user token. Reading security.json exposes the HS256 JWT signing secret and password hashes, allowing an attacker to forge an administrator token. Administrative access to POST /skServer/providers can then create an Execute provider that runs commands with the server process privileges and persists its configuration across restarts. This issue is fixed in Signal K Server 2.34.0 and @signalk/resources-provider 1.5.3.

items.title: Nuxt UI is an intuitive Vue UI library powered by Reka UI and Tailwind CSS.
items.description: Nuxt UI is an intuitive Vue UI library powered by Reka UI and Tailwind CSS. Prior to 4.8.1, the server-rendered form element produced by UForm in src/runtime/components/Form.vue omits the method and action attributes and relies solely on the hydrated @submit.prevent handler to stop native submission. UAuthForm composes UForm and can render named credential fields, including an input with type password, inside the same markup. If a user submits before Vue hydration completes, or when the client bundle is blocked or unavailable, the browser performs its default GET submission and serializes the named fields into the current URL query string. The credentials can then appear in the address bar, browser history, reverse-proxy, CDN, or WAF request logs, and Referer headers sent with same-origin subresource requests. This issue is fixed in version 4.8.1.

items.title: Dynatrace MCP Server is an MCP server for Dynatrace Observability.
items.description: Dynatrace MCP Server is an MCP server for Dynatrace Observability. Prior to 2.0.0, the create_workflow_for_notification tool inserts the caller-controlled teamName, problemType, and channel values into a Dynatrace workflow without neutralizing Jinja2 expressions. A caller can place template expressions such as event() in those values, and the workflow engine evaluates them when the persistent workflow runs. When the workflow has a valid Slack connector, the resulting Slack action can disclose event or tenant metadata to an attacker-selected channel; the shipped placeholder connection does not deliver messages by itself. The workflow remains in the tenant after the MCP session and credentials are gone. The isPrivate option defaults to false, making the created workflow tenant-visible unless the caller changes it. Exploitation requires either an MCP prompt-injection path or an operator approving a prompt that displays the template fragment literally. This issue is fixed in version 2.0.0.

items.title: python-tuf is a Python reference implementation of The Update Framework (TUF).
items.description: python-tuf is a Python reference implementation of The Update Framework (TUF). Prior to 7.0.0, DelegatedRole._is_target_in_pathpattern in tuf/api/_payload.py uses fnmatch.fnmatch, which applies os.path.normcase before matching and makes delegation path authorization case-insensitive on Windows. When a TUF repository has path-based delegations that differ only by case and an attacker-controlled role is visited before the legitimate role, ngclient can accept an attacker-provided target from the wrong delegation for a requested path. Linux and macOS clients are not affected because their path normalization does not change case. This issue is fixed in 7.0.0.

items.title: A flaw was found in OpenSCAP.
items.description: A flaw was found in OpenSCAP. A heap-based buffer overflow can occur when processing a specially crafted Extensible Configuration Checklist Description Format (XCCDF) document using the sds-compose option. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability to corrupt memory, resulting in an application crash and a Denial of Service (DoS).

items.title: TrailBase 0.28.2 before 0.35.10 contains an insecure direct object reference in std.FileUpload columns, where the Recor…
items.description: TrailBase 0.28.2 before 0.35.10 contains an insecure direct object reference in std.FileUpload columns, where the Record API accepts attacker-supplied object-store file ids on insert and update without ownership validation. An authenticated attacker who can read a victim’s row can recover its stripped file id via a $like filter and then permanently delete or orphan the victim’s file by deleting or nulling a record they own.

items.title: Monoceros versions before 0.30 for Perl allow a request declaring a large Content-Length to kill a worker by exhausting…
items.description:
Monoceros versions before 0.30 for Perl allow a request declaring a large Content-Length to kill a worker by exhausting memory.

The request body is read in a loop that asks sysread for all of the remaining declared length at once. Perl grows the read buffer to that size before any data arrives, so a length larger than available memory makes the worker exit with an uncatchable out of memory error before the application is called.

A remote attacker can force a worker restart with each request of a few bytes.

items.title: Incorrect permission assignment allows local privilege escalation to SYSTEM on affected releases of the Illumio VEN for…
items.description: Incorrect permission assignment allows local privilege escalation to SYSTEM on affected releases of the Illumio VEN for Windows. Code execution as NT AUTHORITY\LOCAL SERVICE on the Windows host is required to exploit this vulnerability. The flaw exists within the VEN installer, which grants LOCAL SERVICE full access to the VEN data and installation folders, whose configuration and state files are read and trusted by the SYSTEM-privileged illumio-ven-ctl component. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to modify the VEN configuration so that illumio-ven-ctl executes an injected command in the context of the SYSTEM account.

items.title: ModSecurity is an open source, cross platform web application firewall (WAF) engine for Apache, IIS and Nginx.
items.description: ModSecurity is an open source, cross platform web application firewall (WAF) engine for Apache, IIS and Nginx. Prior to 2.9.15 and 3.0.17, msre_fn_removeComments_execute in apache2/re_tfns.c and inplace() in src/actions/transformations/remove_comments.cc implement t:removeComments by copying the character immediately after a comment terminator without re-evaluating it. Adjacent comments can therefore leave a later comment in the transformed value, allowing inline-comment obfuscation to bypass rules that depend on comment stripping. When a comment terminator is the final content, the same copy reads one byte beyond the input buffer. This issue is fixed in versions 2.9.15 and 3.0.17.

items.title: AsyncSSH is a Python package which provides an asynchronous client and server implementation of the SSHv2 protocol on t…
items.description: AsyncSSH is a Python package which provides an asynchronous client and server implementation of the SSHv2 protocol on top of the Python asyncio framework. Prior to 2.24.1, SFTPServer.map_path() uses posixpath.normpath() on a client-supplied path and removes only one leading slash before passing the result to posixpath.join() with the configured chroot. An authenticated SFTP user can supply a path beginning with exactly two slash characters, causing POSIX normalization to preserve the double-leading-slash form and the subsequent join to treat the remaining pathname as absolute. This bypasses the SFTP chroot and permits reads and writes with the operating-system permissions of the account running the server, which may enable code execution depending on writable targets. This issue is fixed in version 2.24.1.

items.title: zizmor: Debug logging prints available GitHub credentials in cleartext
items.description: zizmor is a static analysis tool for CI/CD systems. In version 1.27.0, debug logging serializes the parsed application configuration with a derived Debug implementation for GitHubToken, causing credentials supplied through GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, ZIZMOR_GITHUB_TOKEN, --gh-token, --github-token, or --zizmor-github-token to be written to stderr in cleartext. A single -v or --verbose option or an applicable RUST_LOG directive enables the affected logging during normal online operation and --no-online-audits, while explicit --offline clears the token first. If another party can read a CI log, support artifact, terminal capture, or public bug report containing the output, the party can use the credential according to its scopes, repository access, and lifetime. This vulnerability is fixed in 1.28.0.

items.title: GPUStack GPUStack: GPUStack Improper Authentication Vulnerability
items.description:
### Impact

In GPUStack before v2.2.0, `get_current_user` (in `gpustack/api/auth.py`) promotes any request whose source is considered loopback to the built-in administrator account when `force_auth_localhost` is `False` (the default). The "source" is derived by `client_ip_getter`, which can be made to report `127.0.0.1` without any credentials in two ways:

1. **Same-host reverse proxy (TCP peer).** In the canonical self-hosted shape —
   GPUStack behind a same-host reverse proxy with `proxy_pass
   http://127.0.0.1:<port>` — every remote request arrives at GPUStack with TCP
   peer `127.0.0.1`, so the loopback auto-admin branch fires. No header or
   credential is required. Verified end-to-end against HEAD `6bee5883`.
2. **`X-GPUStack-Real-IP` header.** A forged `X-GPUStack-Real-IP: 127.0.0.1`
   header can cause the request source to be treated as loopback.

Either path yields **full, unauthenticated administrative access** over the network: enumerate and modify users, models, workers, and configuration; mint persistent admin API keys (scope `["*"]`, valid from any source IP thereafter); read worker credentials and cloud/provider secrets. Combined with admin-only functionality such as `POST /v2/inference-backends/from yaml`, this leads to code execution on worker hosts.

This vulnerability has been observed exploited in the wild against a v2.1.1 deployment (attacker-created custom backends running reverse shells).

### Root cause

Trusting the network source of a request (socket peer, or a client-controllable header) as an authentication signal. When GPUStack is fronted by a same-host reverse proxy, the socket peer is always loopback, so the "localhost is trusted" assumption no longer holds.

### Patches

Fixed in `gpustack` `2.2.0`: the loopback auto-admin path was removed and client-IP / forwarding-header handling was hardened. Upgrade to `2.2.0` or later.

### Workarounds

- Set `force_auth_localhost=true` to require authentication even for loopback
  requests.
- Ensure the reverse proxy / gateway cannot cause GPUStack to treat external
  traffic as loopback, and strip any client-supplied `X-GPUStack-Real-IP`
  header at the edge.
- Keep the API off untrusted networks (VPN / edge authentication).

### Remediation (in the fix)

Do not derive authentication from the request's network source. Remove implicit loopback-based admin, and only accept a real client-IP header from an authenticated/trusted gateway (never from arbitrary clients).

### Credit

Independently reported by Nikko Enggaliano; Wei Yunzhou; and Rui Yang & Haoyu Wang (Johns Hopkins University). Active in the-wild exploitation was reported by Javier Sixto (ulex.fr).

### Impact
Host header injection risk when using Omniauth with a web framework that does not verify incoming host headers.
